articles.title: Poland Drafts ‘Pre-War’ Readiness Law to Speed Up Allied Troop Deployment
articles.body:
Poland’s Defense Ministry is drafting legislation that would prepare the state for a “pre-war” phase of full defense readiness, allowing troops and institutions to mobilize before martial law is formally declared.
This was confirmed by the ministry’s media department to the Polish Rzeczpospolita on Friday, Oct. 2. The draft is currently in internal consultations and, until recently, its working title referred to the state’s defense readiness “for war.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The legislation aims “to strengthen the defense capabilities of the Republic of Poland, improve cooperation between the armed forces and the services responsible for internal security, and adapt existing regulations to contemporary threats, in particular hybrid, cyber and disinformation threats,” the ministry told Rzeczpospolita.
Line between hybrid and direct attacks increasingly blurs
The bill is designed to cover the period between regular peacetime operations and a formal declaration of martial law.
A source linked to the presidential office told the newspaper that the decision reflects the “pre-war” period Prime Minister Donald Tusk had previously warned about.
Under the draft, Poland would be able to deploy troops, including allied forces, to critical areas earlier than current rules allow. It would also link the country’s Defense Response Plan with NATO’s Response System and set out steps to prepare infrastructure for heightened readiness.
Putin’s Pantsir Problem: Why Russia’s Air Defense Is Failing
According to Rzeczpolita, the law would expand the number of institutions involved in permanent duty arrangements and in the national defense command system.
It would also introduce rules for civilian staff working in command posts with limited ability to return home, alongside changes to non-military operational planning, defense training, courses and exercises.
The Defense Ministry, led by Deputy Prime Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, said it was not yet known when the bill would reach the Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament, citing the complexity of the legislative process.
The National Security Bureau (BBN), which advises the president, is also awaiting the draft, according to Rzeczpospolita.
Scattered regulations
The ministry said current rules on defense preparations are spread across several government ordinances adopted after the parliament passed the Homeland Defense Act in spring 2022.
This approach allegedly makes it more difficult to ensure a uniform approach to defense tasks across public institutions. Regulations are also harder to keep consistent. Because some of the provisions directly define the duties and powers of state bodies, the ministry argues they should be set out in law rather than in ordinances.
According to Polish media, the current framework dates back to March 18, 2025 when the government replaced a 2004 regulation and reduced the number of defense readiness states from three to two.
The state of permanent defense readiness applies in peacetime and covers planning, training, warning systems and preparations against hybrid threats such as cyberattacks and disinformation.
The state of full defense readiness can be introduced in response to an external threat or in wartime, enabling mobilization and the full deployment of the country’s defense system.
The government must request that change from the president.
Earlier law did not account for modern challenges
Grzegorz Matyasik, a security expert at the Eastern Flank Institute and former deputy director of Poland’s Government Security Center, told the newspaper that the new initiative shows the 2022 Homeland Defense Act was poorly drafted.
According to him, the law had largely copied earlier provisions without accounting for modern challenges, including hybrid threats.
Any new regulation should also cover crisis management and the protection of critical infrastructure, he said, adding that this should be closely coordinated with the Government Security Center and the Interior Ministry.
The conclusion was that Poland still lacks a dedicated law on state resilience.
Michał Dworczyk, vice-chair of the European Parliament’s Security and Defense Committee, said that while he had not yet seen the draft, organizing scattered and often unclear regulations was the right approach, provided the changes were sensible and properly consulted.
“We are dealing with an unpredictable adversary, the Russian Federation, which constantly violates international law and agreements,” Dworczyk said, according to Rzeczpolita.
He added that Poland should urgently assess whether its crisis management capabilities could cope with further Russian escalation.
Tensions continue to grow
The draft follows months of escalation and repeated warnings from Tusk that Russia could extend its war onto NATO territory.
In July, he said the upcoming months may prove “critical,” adding that such concerns were particularly palpable in the Baltic states.
Mid-September, he repeated his concerns, warning that intelligence indicated Moscow was planning drone and missile strikes on countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland – which it could present as accidental in an effort to weaken NATO’s resolve.
Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev threatened Lithuania on Sept. 11, saying that the country would disappear from the map of the world should it lift its ban on nuclear weapons. He claimed NATO would not invoke Article 5, as that would mean “a global catastrophe.”
Days later, Kremlin aide Nikolai Patrushev threatened to use Russia’s “entire arsenal” against Poland, claiming that “Warsaw will disappear in two or three days,” after Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski said NATO could quickly defeat Moscow if attacked.
Meanwhile, Moscow has dismissed claims that it is preparing to attack NATO, even as its officials continue to escalate their rhetoric toward the alliance.
Russian President Vladimir Putin repeated unfounded claims about the mistreatment of Russian-speaking minorities in the Baltic states on Sept. 25, the same pretext the Kremlin used to justify its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Just two days later, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov claimed that European preparations for a possible war with Russia could prove to be a “self-fulfilling prophecy,” simultaneously dismissing warnings of a Russian attack as “nonsense.”
In recent days, tensions between the Kremlin and NATO’s eastern flank have also escalated sharply over Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave, which borders Poland and Lithuania.
On Monday, Sept. 28, Moscow warned NATO it was ready to use its entire arsenal if the alliance tried to isolate the territory. Putin repeated the threat by raising nuclear weapons again on Thursday, Oct. 1, warning that Russia would respond if attacked and that citizens of the EU should “be fully aware of that.”
NATO spokesperson Allison Hart condemned Russia’s nuclear rhetoric and noted that the alliance was exclusively defensive.
Moscow’s remarks, however, echo the same rhetoric used in the months before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, when the Kremlin repeatedly dismissed Western warnings of an imminent attack as false, while justifying its actions with claims that it needed to protect Russian speakers.
Even after five years of war, the Kremlin continues downplaying its aggression as a “special military operation.”

articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1682: Russian drones repeatedly hit Kyiv’s Southern Bridge, forcing transport restrictions across the capital
articles.body:
Exclusives
Military
Russia repeatedly attacks bridge connecting Kyiv's two sides across the Dnipro river, disrupting transport across the capital. The Southern Bridge has come under repeated Russian drone attacks since 1 October, forcing transport restrictions as Russia steps up daily attacks with jet-powered Geran drones.
Russia paid with more than 46,000 casualties, and the front moved the other way, ISW finds. September ended with a net Russian territorial loss, the think tank says.
Drones hit Russia's Volgograd and Samara overnight—fires near a Lukoil refinery, a chemical plant, and likely Europe's largest oil tank farm in Samara. The Samara station blends crude from four trunk pipelines into Urals, Russia's flagship export grade.
Spain, Belgium, and Poland are sending Ukraine F-16 cannon rounds to fight Russia's jet drones. A much larger 20-mm package may follow, and Kyiv is also negotiating with private manufacturers.
Russia lost 2026-record 46,230 troops in September by Ukraine's count, as fighting around Donetsk fortress cities grinds on. At the same time, Russia's strikes on Ukraine's rear escalated in September and are climbing again in October.
Belgium will send three F-16 fighter jets, but maintenance delays may keep Ukraine from using them. The likely reason is the lengthy maintenance process, which may keep many of the jets from shooting down Russian drones and cruise missiles attacking Ukraine.
Ukraine is downing Russia's fastest drones—just not often enough, and scaling up comes down to money. Russia's jet drones outrun the cheap interceptors Ukraine built for slower Shaheds, pushing Kyiv to field new hardware that works in combat but can't yet be made in the numbers its skies demand.
Russia just accidentally crashed its first Tu-95 bomber in 11 years. Its missiles will keep striking Ukraine anyway. It is out of production and Russia's bomber fleet keeps shrinking, but a raid on 8 September needed just six bombers, and Russia still has around a hundred.
Intelligence and technology
Ukraine turned ground robots into a frontline workhorse. Its first competitive tender may reward cheap copies over proven machines, an officer warns. Kyiv opened its first competitive tender for logistics and strike robots—a model a frontline officer warns rewards the cheapest compliant bid and could favor cheap copies over proven machines.
Ukrainian firm fields 11 crewless boats and eight drones at NATO's biggest naval drone drill. UFORCE's crews acted as both attacker and defender at the REPMUS 26 drills, where Portugal's president came to inspect one of the company's boats on the dock.
Ukraine's former defense minister, dismissed suddenly, has announced Army of Robots. He says target is $10,000 per unit and need is tens of thousands. His "Army of Robots" would have machines carry ammunition, pull out the wounded, clear mines, and hold positions, the roles that cost soldiers their lives.
Europe wants drones that actually work in war, so Ukrainian maker is moving in to build them in Belgium and Luxembourg. TAF Industries and Luxembourg's LUXUAV signed a memorandum to develop and field drones.
Ukraine solves riddle of metal "whiskers" on new Russia's drones. They aren't clever sensor. The metal prongs appearing on Russian strike drones are a mechanical contact detonator.
Robots won't replace armored vehicles, says Ukrainian company that builds both. It reveals one job they can't do. Ukraine ran 100,000 robot missions this year.
International
Russia retaliates after Hungary expels 10 diplomats, deepening Budapest-Moscow rift since Orbán's ouster. The diplomatic tit-for-tat comes as Hungary's new government takes a markedly different approach to Russia and Ukraine from Viktor Orbán's 16-year tenure.
Sanctions keep catching Russia's gas tankers, so Moscow is building new ones, UK says. Britain unveiled 31 new sanctions, aiming to squeeze Moscow's finances before winter sets in.
Ukraine's steel output fell 57% and may hit zero next month. Expert says saving it comes down to four steps, and they're Brussels' to make. Steel is Ukraine's second-largest foreign-currency earner, employing more than 70,000 people directly and another 250,000 in related industries.
Moscow's message to European business: your Russian assets are now leverage against your governments. ISW expects decisions on which firms to seize to depend entirely on Russia's relations with each company's home country.
There is no risk of Russia using nuclear weapons against the Baltics, Rutte assures. Rutte's assessment comes as Moscow warns the alliance that isolating Kaliningrad could trigger a nuclear response.
The US has until 18 October to choose its Russia sanctions targets—if any. Kyiv's wish list leads with the firms feeding Russia's Starlink clone. At the top: Russian firms making parts for Moscow's Starlink rival, still untouched by US sanctions.
Humanitarian and social impact
41 Ukrainians made the long journey from occupation to Ukrainian-controlled territory after enduring Russian pressure, detention and control. Four children and five teenagers were among those who returned to Ukraine in August and September through a route via Belarus.
Ukrainian grandmother detained in Kazakhstan at Russia's request while trying to bring grandson back to Ukraine. Russia used the Russia-led CSTO to pursue the Ukrainian citizen beyond its borders, triggering her detention in Kazakhstan and potentially exposing her to deportation to Russia.
A school with children, a café, warehouses: Russia's drones hit civilian Kyiv again. More than 100 students and about 60 staff were in the school's shelter when a Russian drone hit the building. All came through unharmed, as fires burned across two Kyiv districts.
Russian glide bombs scarred a statue of Christ and damaged a 19th-century church in Sumy. The same strike hit a school where children were sheltering and nearby homes, where two people were killed and six injured, three of them children.
Political and legal developments
Ukraine files a minority-schooling bill, and Hungary agrees to unblock two of its EU-accession clusters. The Rada plans to vote on 12 October, and under the deal, Hungary is to stop blocking two EU-accession clusters once the bill is law.
Russia's 2026 deficit nearly doubles to a record $88 billion, and its new budget plans three more years in the red. The draft sent to the Duma still gives the military its biggest budget since the full-scale invasion began.
Two rubles for the army for every one on welfare, schools, and hospitals: Russia's 2027 wartime budget. Civilian spending is set to fall to about 9% of GDP, a level not seen since 2005.
Read our previous daily review here.

- Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1679: Russia raises its war budget by 27% to a record as it looks to grow its war in 2027

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Russia takes aim at key Kyiv bridge for second day
articles.body:
Key developments on Oct. 2:
- Key Kyiv bridge hit by Russian drones fourth time in 2 days
- Ukraine aims to produce up to 400 interceptor drones as Russian jet-powered drone use grows, Zelensky says
- UK sanctions 7 Russians over deportation, indoctrination of Ukrainian children
- Russian Mi-8 helicopter reportedly shot down in friendly-fire incident over Voronezh Oblast
- Russian glide bombs strike Kharkiv, kill women, injure children
- Russia planning to increase "hybrid warfare" activity in Europe, Ukrainian intelligence warns
A Russian drone struck the Southern Bridge over the Dnipro River in Kyiv around 5:40 p.m. local time, as Russia takes aim at the bridge for two days straight.
At the time of the fourth drone strike, the bridge was still closed for traffic from an earlier attack in the morning, said Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko. Black smoke could be seen rising over the bridge, while the damage to the structure is not yet determined.
The Russian attack coincided with Kyiv's evening rush hour, adding further stress to the already congested city. Kyiv's other main bridges across the Dnipro River, the Darnytskyi Bridge, Metro Bridge, and Podilskyi Bridge, have been changed to single direction traffic, according to the Kyiv City Military Administration (KMDA).
Kostiantyn Kryvolap, an aviation expert and former Antonov test engineer, told the Kyiv Independent that destruction of the bridge is most likely not the intent behind Russia's strikes.
"Destroying a bridge with a 50-kilogram explosive charge, even with a highly effective warhead designed to destroy steel bridge structures, is a major exaggeration. It is practically impossible. For a bridge like this, these strikes are more like mosquito bites," he said.
Instead, the idea behind the Russian strikes may rather be to halt traffic, interrupt logistics, and exert psychological pressure on Kyiv's population, according to him.
The Southern Bridge is one of the capital's main traffic arteries and connects important transport routes like the the M-05 Kyiv-Odesa, M-06 Kyiv-Chop, and M-03 Kyiv-Kharkiv-Izyum-Sloviansk highways. Every day, between 100,000 and 110,000 cars use the bridge, according to information from the Darnytskyi District administration from 2019.
Head of the Desnyanskyi district of Kyiv, Maksym Bakhmatov, told The Village in a 2020 interview that about 90% of transit traffic between the two banks passes through the Southern Bridge.
Hlib Vyshlinsky, executive director of the Center for Economic Strategy told the Kyiv Independent that the Southern Bridge is also crucial for the daily commute of the Pozniaky-Osokorky-Kharkivsky districts conglomeration that houses up to 500,000 people.

Ukraine aims to produce up to 400 interceptor drones as Russian jet-powered drone use grows, Zelensky says
Ukraine will be able to produce up to 400 interceptor drones by the end of October to counter Russia's growing use of jet-powered attack drones, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview with the Financial Times published on Oct. 2.
As Russia scales up production of its jet-powered drones — the Geran-4 and Geran-5 — Ukraine is struggling to shoot them down amid the hours-long attacks.
Russia launched around 500 drones against Ukraine over the past day, about half of which were jet-powered and significantly harder to intercept, Zelensky said.
Only 57% of jet-powered versions of Shahed-type drones are currently shot down by Ukraine, Zelensky said in his evening address on Sept. 28, a figure he described as "much less than necessary."
According to Zelensky, Ukraine is testing five types of high-speed interceptor drones designed to counter Russian weapons. One of the models is expected to reach production of around 400 units by the end of October, while the other four remain in the testing stage.
The development of the interceptors is being slowed by a shortage of engines. Ukraine imports most of the engines used for the drones, while domestic production remains insufficient, Zelensky said.
Russia's jet-powered drones target civilian infrastructure such as supermarkets, schools, shopping malls, telecommunications infrastructure, data centers, gas stations, and medical facilities.
Russia has increased its use of jet-powered drones while launching attacks on Kyiv in recent months. The onslaught began last month but has intensified over the past week.
read also
UK sanctions 7 Russians over deportation, indoctrination of Ukrainian children
The U.K. sanctioned seven Russian individuals involved in the forced deportation and re-education of Ukrainian children from occupied territories on Oct. 1, the Ukrainian President's initiative, Bring Kids Back, said on Oct. 2.
Russia is militarizing Ukrainian children and youth in the occupied territories, removing their Ukrainian identity to "raise future soldiers" and involve them in the fight against their own people.
Russia has abducted tens of thousands of Ukrainian children since the start of the full-scale invasion. As of September 2026, Ukraine's Justice Ministry has officially confirmed 20,610 cases of deportation, though Ukrainian officials estimate the real total could number in the hundreds of thousands.
According to Bring Kids Back's press release, the sanctions target Artur Orlov, head of Russia's Movement of the First, a state-backed organization for children and young people, as well as five heads of its regional branches in occupied parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts and Crimea.
The Movement of the First was established in 2022 at the initiative of Russian President Vladimir Putin and has more than 344,600 members in occupied Ukrainian territories, according to a report from an Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) expert mission.
The sanctioned officials are Denis Chernobay, Ruyal Aliyev, Aleksey Lavrentyev, Viktoriya Kostromina, and Ekaterina Kozyr.
The list also includes Elena Milskaya, chair of the board of trustees of Russia's National Center for Assistance to Missing and Injured Children. Ukraine's military intelligence agency said Milskaya used the organization's volunteers in October 2022 to facilitate the mass abduction and unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children, including orphans, from occupied territories to Russia's Krasnodar Krai via occupied Crimea.
The sanctioned individuals face asset freezes and travel bans, as well as restrictions on trust services and director disqualification. At least three of the seven — Orlov, Chernobay, and Milskaya — have previously been sanctioned by Canada, while Milskaya has also been sanctioned by the European Union.
The U.K. announced the sanctions on Oct. 1 as part of a wider package targeting 31 individuals over Russia's war against Ukraine. The package also includes eight people accused of involvement in arbitrary detention, torture, and ill-treatment of civilians in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories, including Kherson and Zaporizhzhia oblasts.
read also
Russian Mi-8 helicopter reportedly shot down in friendly-fire incident over Voronezh Oblast
A Russian Su-35 fighter jet reportedly shot down a Russian Mi-8 military helicopter in a friendly-fire incident in Russia's Voronezh Oblast on Oct. 1, killing all three crew members, according to several Russian and Ukrainian Telegram channels.
The helicopter crashed in the Anninsky district of Voronezh Oblast, around 80 kilometers from the regional capital, while Russian forces were responding to a supposed Ukrainian drone attack, according to reports.
The Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova Plus said the Su-35 crew mistakenly identified the Mi-8 as a Ukrainian drone and opened fire. The helicopter's pilot, navigator, and onboard gunner were killed, according to the channel.
Another Ukrainian Telegram channel, Dossier of a Spy, also said that the Mi-8 was mistakenly shot down by a Su-35 during a drone attack.
Russian military blogger Ilya Tumanov, who runs the Fighterbomber Telegram channel, reported the loss of the helicopter without directly identifying the cause.
The reports have not been independently verified, and Russian authorities have not publicly confirmed that the Mi-8 was shot down by the fighter jet.
read also
Russian glide bombs strike Kharkiv, kill women, injure children
At least two people were killed and 36 injured after Russian glide bombs struck two areas of the city of Kharkiv on the afternoon of Oct. 2.
"Three glide bombs were recorded hitting the Slobidskyi and Nemyshlyansky districts of the city," Oleh Syniehubov, head of the Kharkiv Regional State Administration, said in a statement on Telegram.
"Two women aged 66 and 80 died as a result of the strike by the Russian army. 32 people were injured," Syniehubov said.
The State Emergency Service (DSNS) in Kharkiv later raised the number of injured to 36. Three of the injured were children, according to DSNS.
One of the Russian glide bombs "completely destroyed" a residential building, Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov said in a statement.
read also
Russia planning to increase "hybrid warfare" activity in Europe, Ukrainian intelligence warns
Russia's secret services have been tasked with increasing the number of attacks in Europe, Ukrainian military intelligence (HUR) warned in a statement on Oct. 2.
"The special services of the aggressor state of Russia have been tasked with increasing activity on the territory of the European Union and NATO states — this involves preparing for hybrid operations aimed at undermining aid to Ukraine and weakening the Alliance's capabilities," the statement says.
Acts of Russian "hybrid warfare" have included arson, assassinations, and a recent attempt to blow up Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft with modified FPV drones in Leipzig in August. On Sept. 1, Germany formally accused Russia of carrying out the attack.
"To carry out operations, including sabotage operations, the Kremlin plans to involve agents recruited by the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces (GRU) and the FSB of the Russian Federation in Europe. The Russian special services are targeting military facilities, critical infrastructure, and communication systems," the statement says.
"Among the aggressor's likely targets are Starlink satellite internet receiving stations located in European countries," HUR said.
Starlink, manufactured and operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX, is widely used for communications by the Ukrainian military.
European governments are stepping up preparations for possible Russian hybrid attacks as officials across the continent warn that Moscow could increasingly use drones, missiles, sabotage, and cyberattacks to test NATO countries and pressure them over their support for Ukraine.
"The Ukrainian Defense Ministry's Directorate of Defense warned its partners about the criminal plans of the aggressor state of Russia," the statement says.

articles.title: Russian Drill Simulates Incursion and ‘Security Zone’ in Tsentr-2026 Games
articles.body:
Russian armed forces practiced transitioning from defensive operations to a counter-offensive and carving out a “security zone” inside the territory of a neighboring state during the large-scale strategic military exercise Tsentr-2026, according to official Kremlin dispatches and Russian defense ministry briefings.
The maneuvers, conducted between Sept. 28 and Oct. 3, were formally designated to practice repelling conventional aggression on the Central Asian strategic vector and ensuring military security across the Caspian Sea basin.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
However, operational details presented to Russian President Vladimir Putin revealed that the drills incorporated cross-border offensive actions.
Reporting to Putin on the progress of the maneuvers, Russian Deputy Defense Minister Yunus-Bek Yevkurov stated that after repelling an adversary’s opening assault, coalition forces launched a large-scale counter-offensive.
Yevkurov detailed that starting Oct. 2, troops rehearsed operations to “liberate seized territory” and establish a “security zone on adjacent territory” belonging to the opposing state.
Putin traveled in person to the Chebarkul military training ground in the Chelyabinsk region on Friday, Oct. 2, to observe the concluding phase of the exercises, stating that Russian formations were directly integrating operational tactics and doctrine developed during the full-scale war in Ukraine.
Russia Plans Record $200B Defense Budget as Healthcare, Education, Face Cuts
Central Asian vector
While Russian defense officials did not formally name the hypothetical neighboring adversary, defense analysts at Ukrainian military portal Militarnyi noted that Kazakhstan most closely matches the operational geography of the scenario.
Kazakhstan shares an extensive land border with Russia’s Chelyabinsk region where the Chebarkul training facility is situated, represents a central political entity in Central Asia, and possesses an extensive coastline along the Caspian Sea.
Analysts emphasized that while the operational design closely mirrors regional geography, the identification of Kazakhstan remains an analytical assessment rather than an officially confirmed element of Moscow’s war games.
The strategic maneuvers involved significant firepower across multiple domains. Four Russian long-range strategic bombers conducted simulated strikes against designated “critical infrastructure” of the adversary, supported by tactical aviation, artillery units, strike drones, mechanized armored columns, and surface combatants of the Caspian Flotilla.
According to Russian defense ministry figures, the Tsentr-2026 exercise mobilized more than 47,000 military personnel, over 2,000 pieces of heavy weaponry and military hardware, 90 combat and transport aircraft, and 77 naval ships and support vessels.
Operations were executed across 11 designated military ranges and the maritime zone of the Caspian Sea. Moscow additionally hosted foreign military contingents from Belarus, China, Kyrgyzstan, Mongolia, Pakistan, and Tajikistan.
European pre-war legislation
The offensive maneuvers in Central Asia coincide with heightened defense vigilance across NATO’s eastern flank, where frontline European governments are preparing for prospective cross-border escalation.
In Poland, the Ministry of National Defense confirmed on Friday that it is drafting comprehensive legislation to introduce a formal “pre-war” phase of defense readiness, enabling early troop deployments and institutional mobilization before martial law is legally declared.
The draft statute is designed to bridge the regulatory gap between peacetime governance and wartime mobilization, linking national operational plans directly to NATO’s Response System.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has repeatedly warned that Europe has entered a “pre-war era,” cautioning that allied intelligence dispatches indicate Moscow is evaluating hybrid drone and missile strikes against nations supporting Kyiv, which the Kremlin could portray as accidents to test the resolve of NATO’s Article 5 collective defense guarantee.
The legislative drive also follows escalatory rhetoric from senior Russian officials directed at frontline European states. Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev threatened Lithuania in September with destruction if it rescinded restrictions on nuclear weapons, asserting NATO would not risk global war to defend Vilnius.
Days later, Kremlin security aide Nikolai Patrushev threatened that Moscow could deploy its “entire arsenal” against Poland, claiming Warsaw could be destroyed within days following Polish warnings that the alliance would decisively defeat any conventional Russian attack.

articles.title: UK plays the blame game, terror in the skies, Russia’s red lines: RT stories that shaped the week
articles.body:
UK plays the blame game, terror in the skies, Russia’s red lines: RT stories that shaped the week
The terror plot that wasn’t
The arrest of five men at RAF Fairford in the UK on Sunday sparked a terror panic whose consequences are still playing out almost a week later. Shortly after the arrests, British Foreign Secretary Ed Milliband described the incident as an example of “the threats our country faces,” while the British media’s ‘security experts’ pinned the blame on Iran – or in some cases Russia.
The men – all British nationals aged between 21 and 25 – were released on bail on Monday, and no explosives were found in their vehicles. Nevertheless, Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced on Thursday that “we can confirm our belief that we believe Iran to have played a part.”
“Our belief that we believe” is not the most confident assertion, and this was immediately picked up in Tehran. “I can confirm Iran’s belief that releasing supposed terrorists working for foreign states really says it all. You’re barking up the wrong tree,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote on X.
Counterterror police arrested a British-Iranian dual national in connection with the supposed plot on Thursday, but it’s still unclear whether he’ll be charged.
Russia reveals its red lines
It is unsurprising that the British media immediately used the incident to escalate tensions with Iran and Russia. After days of intensifying war rhetoric from Ukraine’s British and European backers – which RT is tracking in our ‘Escalation Watch’ special – Russia definitively restated its red lines this week.
In a statement released by three of its embassies on Wednesday, the Russian Foreign Ministry said that Moscow “would be ready to use all its arsenal, including nuclear weapons, to defend its territory if NATO countries try to isolate Kaliningrad region from the rest of the country.”
⚡️ Statement by the Embassy of Russia in Ireland (September 29, 2026)
There has been an abundance of talk, recently, from the European political circles that Russia somehow is planning to launch a military invasion of Europe, escalate its alleged hybrid campaign against… pic.twitter.com/eQsrIUFwmL
— Russia in Ireland (@Rus_Emb_Ireland) September 30, 2026
NATO has carried out several military exercises near Kaliningrad this year, and Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski recently called on the bloc’s military chiefs to surge troops to the Kaliningrad border so that Moscow would be “uncertain of what we will do.”
However, Moscow’s statement – the second of its kind this week – was intended to “remind those hotheads in Europe” of Russia’s long-established conditions for the use of nuclear weapons, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov explained on Wednesday. In his speech at the Valdai Discussion Club’s annual forum on Thursday, Russian President Vladimir Putin reiterated that any military action against Kaliningrad would “inevitably” trigger nuclear retaliation.
Western “hotheads,” however, would do well to consider that NATO’s Article 5 – the bloc’s mutual-defense clause – isn’t as clear-cut as it’s sometimes portrayed. As Russian International Affairs Council President Dmitry Trenin wrote for RT this week, it’s “deliberately ambiguous,” heavily mythologized, and doesn’t guarantee US intervention.
Meanwhile, Russia has continued to intensify its strikes on Ukrainian military and dual-use targets, hitting data centers and logistics hubs in Kiev, and ports and warehouses on Ukraine’s Black Sea coast.
Speaking at Valdai, Putin ruled out any kind of ‘energy ceasefire’. With Ukraine striking Russian refineries and sanctions impairing Russia’s ability to export oil, the idea that Moscow “is supposed to stop hitting things that are important to their economy” is “absurd,” the Russian president stated.
The FlyDubai emergency
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s warnings of an imminent attack against the Jewish state were almost realized on Wednesday, when the first officer of a FlyDubai Boeing 737 en route to Tel Aviv allegedly stabbed his captain and attempted to crash the airliner.
Little is known about the incident beyond what the Israeli government and media has shared, but it appears that a group of passengers overpowered the first officer and pulled the jet out of its dive, before two pilots on board took control and landed in Tabuk, in northern Saudi Arabia.
The pilot, Captain Smit Machchhar, has become a national hero in his native India, while the passengers who reportedly stormed the cockpit were lauded by Netanyahu upon arrival in Tel Aviv. Netanyahu has claimed that the first officer had acted based on “Islamist radical indoctrination,” while his government considers the incident an attempted “terrorist attack.”
Although Netanyahu’s ministers have already used the incident to justify – in the words of National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir – taking their war against “Iran, Lebanon, Gaza and Judea and Samaria [the West Bank]... to the next level”, the unanswered questions are piling up, as Middle East analyst Farhad Ibragimov wrote for RT.
Lavrov shuts down the propaganda
Another unanswered question: what exactly do Western leaders mean when they accuse Russia of waging “hybrid war?” The accusation, typically leveled at Russia after drone sightings, fires and accidents at weapons factories, and even natural disasters, is almost never substantiated, yet serves to justify the West’s rearmament and escalating war rhetoric against Moscow.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov refused to play into the narrative when he was questioned by the BBC’s Steve Rosenberg on Tuesday. The British state journalist asked Lavrov if he would admit “that Russia is waging a covert hybrid war against European countries,” but Lavrov flipped the questioning.
“Are you referring to when we destroy the drones and missiles that Britain and continental Europe supply to Ukraine, which are then fired at us?” the Russian foreign minister retorted. “Is that what you mean by hybrid war?”
Rosenberg wasn’t the only Western antagonist humiliated this week. On Tuesday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz suffered the indignity of having to stand beside Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev in Berlin, as Tokayev described Putin as “an outstanding statesman” possessing “the qualities that are most essential for the leader of a great country.”
Merz, fresh from his party’s back-to-back election losses last month, then traveled to Munster on Thursday, where NATO had inexplicably been awarded the ‘Westphalian Peace Prize’. After NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte accepted the award, he and Merz were met with boos, whistles, and chants of “murderers” and “blood on your hands” when they stepped outside to greet the public.
Russia expands its Arctic footprint
Finally, while it’s easy to assume that the world’s great powers have traversed, mapped, and tamed every inch of the Earth’s surface, that’s not the case, and new milestones are still being reached. On Tuesday, the Russian Navy’s Northern Fleet announced that it had traversed the iceberg-filled Shokalsky Strait for the first time in history.
The strait runs between October Revolution Island and Bolshevik Island in the Severnaya Zemlya archipelago, deep inside the Arctic Circle along the strategically important Northern Sea Route.
The Russian Navy group, consisting of the ice-class patrol ship Ivan Papanin, the large landing ship Kondopoga, the salvage tug Pamir, and the naval tanker Sergey Osipov, successfully passed from the Laptev Sea into the Kara Sea, after repeatedly changing course and speed at short notice to avoid icebergs in the treacherous strait.
Russia is invested in the development of the Northern Sea Route, which is the shortest maritime passage between the Asia-Pacific region and northern Europe. Moscow has also renovated some of its Soviet-era military bases along its northern coast, and stepped up military exercises in the Arctic. As the Northern Fleet passed through the Shokalsky Strait this week, its reconnaissance teams practiced amphibious assault maneuvers on the western side of October Revolution Island.

articles.title: Ukrainian Mirage 2000 Downs Russian Cruise Missile With Cannon
articles.body:
A Ukrainian Air Force Mirage 2000-5F multi-role fighter jet has intercepted and destroyed a Russian S8000 “Banderol” compact cruise missile using its onboard 30mm automatic cannon, marking the first confirmed gun kill of the munition type by the French-supplied aircraft.
The close-range interception was reported by French Aid to Europe, an open-source research initiative monitoring Western military assistance delivered to Kyiv, with defense portal Militarnyi independently detailing the engagement.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to military monitoring data, the Ukrainian fighter pilot bypassed conventional guided air-to-air missiles, relying instead on one of the aircraft’s two internal 30mm DEFA 554 automatic cannons.
Each cannon carries an onboard ammunition capacity of 125 rounds and can fire at a rate of up to 1,800 rounds per minute, giving the aircraft rapid close-in ballistic engagement capabilities against low-flying targets.
Downing an aerial target with automatic cannon fire demands close visual proximity and aggressive maneuvering compared to engaging targets at standoff ranges with guided missiles.
According to manufacturer specifications, the Russian Banderol maintains an operational cruising speed between 520 and 560 kilometers per hour, with maximum dash speeds reaching 620 to 650 kilometers per hour across an operational flight range of up to 500 kilometers.
Close-range gun engagement
Military analysts noted that neutralizing high-speed targets with gun rounds offers substantial cost efficiency by conserving scarce and expensive air-to-air munitions.
Russian Ballistic Missiles and Drones Hit Kyiv, Killing 1
At the end of September, France delivered a fresh consignment of MICA heat-seeking and radar-guided air-to-air missiles alongside specialized 30mm high-explosive incendiary rounds to maintain operational readiness across Ukraine’s Mirage fleet.
The S8000 Banderol, developed by Russian defense contractor Kronshtadt, is engineered as a low-cost, compact cruise missile tailored for saturation barrages against urban logistics, transportation hubs, and utility facilities.
The weapon is propelled by a Chinese-manufactured Swiwin micro-turbojet engine and carries a high-explosive fragmentation warhead weighing more than 114 kilograms, containing roughly 49.5 kilograms of high-grade explosive filler.
Its small radar cross-section, low-altitude flight profile, and turbine velocity have posed operational hurdles for mobile ground-based gun crews, requiring the Ukrainian Air Force to commit combat aircraft to patrol interception sectors.
Late-night information: the Mirage 2000-5F was the first western fighter aircraft to destroy a Russian S8000 Banderol cruise missile with the cannon. In 2025, France took 4️⃣ Mirage 2000-5F from its Air Force’s stocks and transferred them to Kyiv. pic.twitter.com/rtg8LMeocP
— French Aid to Europe 🇨🇵 🇪🇺 (@aidefranceukr) October 1, 2026
French fighter fleet
France delivered its initial batch of renovated Mirage 2000 fighters to Ukraine in early 2025, fulfilling commitments announced by French President Emmanuel Macron to reinforce Ukrainian airspace defenses following the earlier supply of American-built F-16 fighters.
Independent defense estimates place the Ukrainian Air Force’s operational Mirage fleet between 12 and 15 airframes.
The delta-wing French aircraft have been integrated into Ukraine’s layered territorial air defense network, tasked with intercepting cruise missiles and loitering munitions while retaining strike capacity to deploy Western standoff ordnance such as SCALP-EG cruise missiles.
In March 2025, a Ukrainian Mirage 2000 recorded its first confirmed operational victory by intercepting a Russian Kh-101 strategic cruise missile.
The fleet has sustained operational strains amid continuous air patrols. In July 2025, a Ukrainian pilot safely ejected from a Mirage 2000 after experiencing an in-flight equipment failure during a defensive sortie, resulting in the loss of the airframe without causing casualties on the ground.

articles.title: Russia Threatens to Strike Defense Plants in NATO Countries
articles.body:
What is fundamentally new about Zakharova’s statement?
Previously, similar statements from Russia mostly concerned targets inside Ukraine or transport convoys within Ukraine. Now, for the first time, Russia is officially and directly threatening defense plants on the territory of NATO and EU countries, which represents a step toward further escalation.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
At the official diplomatic level of the Foreign Ministry, the Kremlin is effectively legitimizing potential Russian strikes against targets in sovereign NATO nations.
In response, EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius stated that if Russia strikes factories on European territory, it would fall under NATO’s Article 5 on collective defense and trigger a military response.
An aide to Kubilius clarified that this refers specifically to a direct Russian strike, rather than the acts of sabotage that have recently increased at EU arms plants.
At present, NATO does not have a clear position on the conditions for invoking Article 5, which undoubtedly encourages Russia to continue escalating and testing the limits.
The implications
It seems that after Zakharova’s statement that European factories producing weapons for Ukraine are potential military targets for Russia, the question of such a strike should no longer be “will it happen?” but rather “when will it happen?”
The trigger for this statement was Poland’s readiness to locate production of Patriot interceptor missiles for Ukraine. Moscow has thus already publicly formulated the argument it could use to justify such a strike.
Switzerland Allocates $162M for 8 Ukraine Recovery Projects
Before Feb. 24, 2022, many analysts were wrong because they tried to determine whether Putin had already made a final decision to go to war. It was more reliable to look at other things: whether the Kremlin had the capabilities, preparations, political justification, and willingness to take risks. The same logic should be applied now.
Russia already has significant strike-drone capabilities, is expanding sabotage operations and drone activity in Europe, is testing NATO’s response, and is now openly identifying European arms factories as potential targets. The threshold for a strike may therefore be lower than it appears.
A particularly important signal would be a shift in Kremlin rhetoric from “we have the right to strike” to “we warned you”: statements that specific countries or factories “will bear responsibility for the consequences” would indicate further preparation for action.
Russia would most likely launch such a strike if it became convinced that NATO’s response would be limited to sanctions, stronger air defenses, additional military assistance to Ukraine, diplomatic measures, or other steps that stopped short of a direct strike on Russian territory.
The risk would increase if Moscow concluded that previous acts of sabotage, cyberattacks, drone incidents, and other operations in Europe had not produced unacceptable consequences for Russia.
For the Kremlin, such episodes have not only operational but also intelligence value: they reveal the speed of the allies’ response, the level of unity, and the practical limits of that response. If the Russian leadership sees that even after Russia’s involvement has been confirmed, the response remains limited, this could reduce the perceived risk of taking the next step.
Such a decision would become more likely if the Kremlin could carry out an attack in a way that made rapid and unequivocal attribution difficult. For Moscow, a scenario in which responsibility could be denied or remain subject to political debate – at least in the initial stage – would be significantly safer.
The first step, therefore, might not be a demonstrative launch of Geran drones from Russian territory but the use of other types of UAVs, sabotage groups, maritime platforms, intermediaries, or other tools that leave room for uncertainty.
Another condition would be political fragmentation within NATO. The Kremlin would likely count on disputes over whether a particular incident constituted an armed attack, whether Article 4 or Article 5 should be invoked, what the response should look like, and whether it is worth risking a broader conflict over a single damaged facility. If Moscow expected a slow or ambiguous decision-making process, this could create a window of opportunity for a limited attack.
Another key factor would be its assessment of the US position. For the Kremlin, what matters is not only America’s formal commitment to NATO but also Washington’s willingness to support a rapid and forceful response to a single limited strike.
Any signs that the US is politically focused on other issues, that Washington and its European allies disagree, or that it is reluctant to broaden the conflict could be perceived by Moscow as favorable conditions for testing the limits of what it can get away with.
As with the war against Ukraine, we are unlikely to see a specific order to launch such a strike. That is why indirect indicators, including rhetoric used to justify it, should be taken seriously. Zakharova’s statement means that a public justification for a possible strike on military-industrial facilities outside Ukraine has likely already been formulated.

articles.title: Russia shows Pantsir air defense on Belarus-built chassis
articles.body:
- Russia showed a Pantsir-S1M air defense system on a Belarusian MZKT-7930-312 chassis during its Tsentr-2026 exercise.
- Belarus reportedly received a 2024 order for 18 such chassis, and Ukraine destroyed one MZKT-based Pantsir near Mariupol in February.
Russia has shown an upgraded Pantsir-S1M air defense system mounted on a Belarus-built MZKT-7930-312 chassis during its Tsentr-2026 strategic exercise, the first official confirmation that the gun-and-missile system now rides on the heavy Minsk-built chassis.
Until now, the configuration was known only from a leaked supply contract and from a single vehicle that Ukrainian drone operators destroyed near Mariupol in February. Russian officials did not say how many Pantsirs have been built on the new chassis, which units operate them, or whether the switch will extend across the fleet.
Tsentr-2026 ran from Sept. 28 to Oct. 3, with its main stage held on Oct. 2 at the Chebarkul training range in Russia’s Chelyabinsk region. President Vladimir Putin watched part of the drills on Oct. 1. Russia’s Defense Ministry said more than 47,000 troops and over 2,000 pieces of equipment took part. Rostec’s “Russian Weapons” project told Rossiyskaya Gazeta that Pantsir systems were demonstrated during the exercise.
The Pantsir combines short-range surface-to-air missiles with twin 30 mm cannons and its own radar. Russia uses it as the inner layer of its air defense, protecting long-range S-300 and S-400 batteries, airfields and other key sites from aircraft, cruise missiles and drones. The standard version sits on an 8×8 KamAZ-6560 truck, with export versions on the German MAN SX45 and some units on Russia’s BAZ-6309.
The MZKT-7930 is a heavy 8×8 military platform built by the Minsk Wheeled Tractor Plant in Belarus. Russia already uses it for some of its most important systems, including the Iskander ballistic missile launcher, the Bastion coastal defense system and elements of the S-400. A Pantsir on the MZKT-7930 first appeared only as a display mock-up at the MAKS air show near Moscow in 2009.
In early 2024, the Belarusian plant received an order from Russia for 18 MZKT-7930-312 chassis to carry Pantsir systems, according to an investigation reported in April by Ukrainian outlet Obozrevatel. That summer, Pantsir maker KBP, based in Tula, reported successful tests of the chassis. The documents showed the trucks would carry the 72V6 combat module used by Russia’s own armed forces, and the investigation said some vehicles may have been finished as an MZKT-7930-415 version with an armored cab and a different windshield layout.
The first visual evidence of the pairing came from the battlefield. In late February, Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces struck a Pantsir-S1 mounted on an MZKT-7930 near the former Azovstal steel plant in Mariupol, The Defence Blog reported. The vehicle carried add-on screens meant to protect it from drone strikes.
Ukraine has made Pantsirs a priority target. Open-source tracking group Oryx had recorded at least 52 Russian Pantsir systems destroyed or damaged, and Ukrainian officials have claimed that about half of Russia’s deployed Pantsirs have been knocked out, a figure that has not been independently verified.

articles.title: How Iran surprised the world?
articles.body:
How Iran surprised the world?
Putin says the whole world is amazed by Iran's courage and resilience
TEHRAN - Russian President Vladimir Putin is not alone in saying that Iran’s resilience in the war with the United States and Israel has surprised the world. From a former head of Britain’s MI6 to senior American analysts, politicians and major international think tanks, a recurring assessment has emerged during the conflict: Iran proved considerably more resilient than many in Washington and Tel Aviv had anticipated.
“The whole world is closely following what is happening and is amazed at the courage and heroism of the Iranian nation and its resilience,” Putin said Thursday at the plenary session of the 23rd annual meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow.
The Russian president also pointed to what he described as a deep pool of experienced personnel within Iran’s administration, armed forces and Islamic Revolution Guards Corps, including people prepared to sacrifice themselves for their country. He said Moscow hoped the Strait of Hormuz would reopen and that what he called illegal sanctions against Iran would be lifted.
Putin’s assessment echoes observations made by a number of Western and international figures since the war began.
‘More resilient than anyone would have expected’
Perhaps the most striking assessment came from Sir Alex Younger, the former head of Britain’s Secret Intelligence Service, or MI6.
Speaking to The Economist in March, Younger said: “The reality is the US underestimated the task.” He added: “In practice, the Iranian regime has been more resilient than I think anyone would have expected.”
Younger attributed part of Iran’s resilience to decisions made before the war to disperse military capabilities and delegate authority for the use of weapons, making it harder for an intensive air campaign to paralyze the country.
He also said Iran had understood the importance of the energy dimension of the conflict and had used the threat to the Strait of Hormuz to “globalize” the war. His conclusion was striking: Iran had “played a weak hand pretty well.”
That assessment was subsequently highlighted by The Guardian, which reported that Younger believed the United States had lost the strategic initiative to Iran. 
 
‘The Iranians have consistently surprised us’
The surprise was not confined to Britain.
Dennis Ross, a veteran US diplomat and former Middle East peace negotiator, made an unusually direct assessment in a Reuters report in September.
“The Iranians have consistently surprised us in terms of their resiliency,” Ross said, arguing that economic and military pressure alone might not force Tehran to retreat.
Ross’s observation came as Washington was attempting to use economic pressure and a naval blockade to force Tehran to alter its position over the Strait of Hormuz. Reuters reported that Iranian leaders appeared prepared to absorb considerable economic pain rather than simply concede under pressure.
The significance of the comment lies in its source: Ross was not describing Iran from Tehran, but from the perspective of a former senior American negotiator who has spent decades dealing with Middle Eastern security and diplomacy.
An Israeli and American miscalculation
The argument that Iran’s resilience was underestimated has also appeared in major international think tanks.
Mohsen Milani, professor of politics at the University of South Florida, wrote for Chatham House that Washington and Tel Aviv correctly assessed some of Iran’s vulnerabilities but “underestimated the resilience of the Iranian state, the cohesion of its elites and institutions and the nationalist surge a foreign attack would unleash.”
According to Milani, the United States and Israel mistook Iran’s regional setbacks and domestic discontent for signs that the state itself was approaching strategic collapse.
Instead, he wrote, Iran “fought with resilience, regionalized the war, [and] weaponized the Strait of Hormuz,” demonstrating that geography could compensate, at least in part, for military weakness.
This distinction is important. The argument is not that Iran avoided severe losses. It is that the damage inflicted by the United States and Israel did not produce the political and strategic effects that some planners had anticipated.
Even Israel’s assessments pointed to unexpected endurance
A March report by The Washington Post, based on a US State Department cable, offered another revealing indication.
According to the cable, Israeli officials privately assessed that Iran was “not cracking” and was willing to “fight to the end” despite the killing of its supreme leader and the continuing US-Israeli bombing campaign.
The report also quoted Suzanne Maloney, an Iran expert at the Brookings Institution, as saying she was surprised that Israeli officials had underestimated the regime’s resilience.
“That really badly informed assumption is interesting given how impressive Israeli intelligence penetration of Iran has been,” Maloney said, arguing that the miscalculation lay at the root of the strategic problems Washington and Tel Aviv encountered.
What surprised the outside world?
The sources point to several distinct dimensions of Iran’s resilience.
1. The political system did not collapse
One of the central assumptions surrounding the opening phase of the war was that the elimination of senior political and military figures could trigger a rapid breakdown of the Iranian state.
That did not happen. Even the Washington Post report based on the US diplomatic cable described the Iran’s state as still holding power and willing to continue fighting.
Putin’s reference to a “deep bench” of experienced officials and commanders points to the same phenomenon from another perspective: the survival of institutional capacity despite the loss of senior figures.
2. Iran retained the ability to respond
The second surprise was military endurance.
The United States and Israel possessed overwhelming advantages in airpower and precision strike capabilities. Yet Iran retained the ability to launch missiles and drones and to continue imposing costs on its adversaries.
Former MI6 chief Younger specifically linked this resilience to the dispersal of military capabilities and the delegation of launch authority before the war.
Senator Dave McCormick, a member of the US Senate Foreign Relations Committee, also acknowledged that Iran had shown “resilience” and said he was surprised by the scale of its missile inventory and accumulated military capabilities.
3. Hormuz became a strategic lever
Perhaps no aspect of the conflict attracted more international attention than the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran could not match the United States ship-for-ship or aircraft-for-aircraft. Instead, it used geography to create a strategic problem that military superiority alone could not easily solve.
The International Institute for Strategic Studies noted that Iran’s ability to disrupt maritime traffic in the strait “defied expectations.”
Milani similarly described Hormuz as the central strategic lever through which Iran regionalized and globalized the conflict.
The consequence was that a war against Iran rapidly became an international energy and shipping crisis.
4. Iran imposed costs beyond the battlefield
Iran’s strategy did not depend solely on surviving air strikes.
The conflict increasingly involved energy infrastructure, shipping routes and the economies of Gulf states. This created a second front in which Iran could exploit geography and asymmetric capabilities.
Younger said Iran had understood the significance of the “energy war” and used the threat to the strait to globalize the conflict.
5. The expected short war became a prolonged confrontation
The ability of Iran to continue resisting also changed the time horizon of the conflict.
Instead of a rapid campaign producing political capitulation, the war evolved into a prolonged confrontation involving military strikes, economic pressure, maritime restrictions and repeated diplomatic efforts.
By September, Reuters was reporting that US economic pressure was imposing severe costs on Iran, but also quoting analysts who believed Tehran might continue enduring those costs rather than concede.
6. National cohesion proved stronger than expected
Another important factor was the reaction of Iranian society to the foreign attack.
Milani argues that the assault generated a nationalist response that strengthened the state’s ability to endure the war. Chatham House likewise identifies the “nationalist surge” unleashed by the attack as one of the factors Washington and Tel Aviv underestimated.
This does not mean that Iranian society was politically uniform. Rather, the evidence suggests that opposition to the government did not automatically translate into support for externally imposed regime change.
7. The conflict exposed the limits of military superiority
The broader lesson identified by several analysts is that overwhelming military superiority does not automatically translate into political success.
The IISS analysis emphasized that Iran had taken severe losses but had deliberately chosen to impose costs on its opponents and on the wider regional economy.
Milani went further, arguing that the war could mark a challenge to the foundations of the US-led security order in the Persian Gulf.
The result is a paradox: Iran suffered military and economic damage, yet the campaign did not produce the rapid strategic collapse that aggressors had anticipated.
A war that changed the calculation
Taken together, these assessments suggest that the most significant surprise has been the gap between the scale of the damage inflicted and the political and strategic outcome that some expected it to produce.
From the former head of MI6 saying Iran was “more resilient than I think anyone would have expected,” to former US negotiator Dennis Ross saying the Iranians have “consistently surprised us,” the recurring theme is clear: Iran proved capable of absorbing an extraordinary level of military pressure, preserving its governing structures, maintaining the capacity to retaliate and using the geography of the Persian Gulf to turn a military confrontation into a much wider strategic and economic crisis.
All of this demonstrates that Trump’s notion and expectation of the Islamic Republic of Iran’s capitulation are nothing more than a fantasy; even if the conflict escalates in the future, this American dream will not come to pass. As Iranian Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi recently stated in an interview, Iran is "fully prepared" for war—even if it proves to be an "apocalyptic war."
It is now up to US: withdraw from the quagmire of war or brace for even greater costs and losses.

articles.title: SOS - Ukraine’s Looming Dark Winter Demands Decisive Action
articles.body:
Russia’s winter playbook is running again, and its logic is evident. Missile and drone attacks have spread from regional power centers to the core of Kyiv’s infrastructure – high-voltage substations and main bridges over the Dnipro River.
Moscow is not trying to hide what it’s doing. The aim is to paralyze the capital, make life there impossible, and choke the supply lines for troops and equipment to the east.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Western sympathy won’t intercept the missiles over the Dnipro, and it certainly won’t turn on heat in a hospital when the power goes out. If Ukraine’s partners really want to help the country survive this winter, then they need to stop offering sympathy and concern and start changing policy.
That starts in Washington. For months, the US administration has operated in a strange operational double standard: Ukraine will defend itself against incoming missiles, but it shouldn’t attack the airfields and bases inside Russia from where those attacks are being launched, nor the energy-generating sites that sustain the Kremlim’s war effort.
For air defense crews to hunt cruise missiles seconds before they collide – rather than blowing up bombers on the tarmac or storming missile depots in Kursk and Belgorod – is a losing strategy. The US must drop all target restrictions on ATACMS soon.
At the same time, Washington should stop tying military aid to slow domestic procurement schedules and instead fund Ukrainian defense factories directly. Kyiv is developing long-range drone missiles and tactical ballistic systems that are cheaper, faster to deploy, and free from foreign political restrictions. Europe, meanwhile, must take greater responsibility for security in its own neighborhood rather than waiting to see what the US Congress does next.
Ukraine Strikes Russian Drone Site, Crossing, Belgorod Hubs
The first fix is air defense. Firing two-million-dollar interceptors at fifty-thousand-dollar Shahed drones is a quick way to run out of ammunition. European partners that own Patriot, NASAMS, and IRIS-T systems need to hand batteries over directly to help cover cities and transit points like the bridges of Kyiv.
To counter daily drone swarms, European funding should go toward building Ukraine’s mobile fire teams. That’s the only way to clear the lower skies without burning through high-end missile stocks amid ballistic threats. Small teams with thermal scopes, pickup trucks, searchlights, and jammers are the only way to get out of there.
The second solution is the grid. Trying to fix up massive, centralized power plants when bombs are still falling is a waste of time and money. European aid needs to stop making those long-term post-attack repairs and focus on physical armor and decentralization.
Electrical transformers, the hardest components to replace, should be housed in reinforced concrete shelters that can take direct shrapnel hits. Aid should target mobile gas turbines, industrial generators, and battery storage units in the cities on the generation side. If a city can run its water pumps and district heating on local micro-grids and the main power plant is destroyed, it loses most of the terror value.
Europe must stop holding back money. Around $200 billion in frozen Russian central bank assets is in European accounts, most of it at Euroclear in Belgium. For years, lawyers have been debating whether to touch this money while Ukrainian cities get flattened. European leaders need to take these assets and not just skim the annual interest but use them directly for Ukrainian weapons buying and grid repairs.
Making the aggressor pay for the damage isn’t just a nice idea; it’s basic common sense. None of these choices require complex diplomacy or grand ideological speeches. They are practical decisions: let Ukrainians hit back at the sites bombing them, give them the hardware they need to keep the power on, and use Russian money to pay for it.
And finally, President Trump should not be allowed to evade implementing the important sanctions law targeting Russia and its partners that Congress finally passed recently, and he signed. Ignoring it is an insult to US democracy and an unfriendly act against Ukraine at a critical moment.
Ukraine has proven for four and a half years that it can hold the line. It is long past time for its partners, even though they have already given critical but inconsistent support, to show the same backbone.
