articles.title: Russia hits major Kyiv bridge, logistics hub in latest attack
articles.body:
Russia struck a key bridge in Kyiv connecting the left and right bank of the Dnipro river overnight Saturday, as Moscow steps up its aerial campaign against Ukraine.
Traffic was suspended on the capital’s Northern Bridge and emergency services were deployed to the scene amid damage to the road and trolleybus cables on the crossing, Kyiv major Vitaly Klitschko said on Saturday. Around 500,000 people commute from the Dnipro’s left bank to the river’s right bank daily, with eight bridges connecting the two sides in total.
That follows several similar attacks by drones on the Southern Bridge in Kyiv in recent days, forcing the temporary suspension of vehicle movement and huge traffic jams.
Advertisement
Russia’s defense ministry confirmed it had carried out the attack, stating the bridge was being used to transport military cargo. It also separately said it had struck the key Hostomel logistics hub and a cargo ship crossing the Black Sea near the southern port of Odessa.
Separately, the UN-linked International Atomic Energy Agency said four strikes in recent days had threatened safety and security” at the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant, including reportedly disabling an off-site radiation monitoring station.
Moscow has stepped up its bombing campaign in recent weeks against Ukraine’s civil and critical infrastructure, targeting residential areas, energy facilities, sea terminals and data centers, setting the stage for a dire winter for Kyiv. In the past week alone, Russia has launched more than 190 missiles and drones, mostly targeting energy infrastructure.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has ordered his troops to abandon the rules of war, Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the FT this week.
Meanwhile, Ukraine is grappling with a yawning financial deficit and shortage of critical weapons. Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi this week said the country faces a $27 billion defense funding gap this year, with Kyiv hoping to cover about $7 billion domestically and looking to partners for the rest.

articles.title: Russian troops liberate 17 communities in Ukraine operation over week — top brass
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 2. /TASS/. Russian troops liberated 17 communities in the Kharkov, Sumy and Zaporozhye Regions and the Donetsk People’s Republic over the week of September 26 - October 2, including three settlements during the past 24 hours in the special military operation in Ukraine, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
"Last week, Battlegroup North units took control of the settlements of Petropavlovka, Lozovaya, Khripuny, Kreidyanka, Shabelnoye, Nesternoye and Rublenoye in the Kharkov Region and yesterday they established control of the settlements of Grachevka and Serdobino in the Kharkov Region through active and decisive operations. <…> In addition, Battlegroup North units took control of the settlements of Maryino, Ulanovo and Tolstodubovo in the Sumy Region and yesterday they gained control of the settlement of Malaya Rybitsa in the Sumy Region. In the Kharkov Region, Battlegroup North units took control of the settlement of Vysokaya Yaruga," the ministry said in a statement.
"During the week, Battlegroup Center units liberated the settlements of Novovodyanoye and Vesyoloye Pole in the Donetsk People’s Republic through active offensive operations. <…> Over the past week, Battlegroup East units kept advancing deep into the enemy’s defenses and liberated the settlement of Yegorovka in the Zaporozhye Region," it said.
Russian troops deliver eight precision strikes on Ukrainian military sites over week
Russian troops delivered one massive and seven combined strikes by precision weapons and unmanned aerial vehicles on Ukrainian logistics and telecommunications centers, electric power generation facilities and Flamingo missile depots over the week, the ministry reported.
"On September 26 - October 2, the Russian Armed Forces delivered one massive and seven combined strikes, hitting logistics and telecommunications centers, electric power generation facilities, transport and port infrastructure used to support the Ukrainian army’s operations, military airfields, sites producing and storing unmanned aerial vehicles, depots with ammunition, ground-based Flamingo cruise missiles, fuel and materiel, and also temporary deployment areas of Ukrainian armed formations and foreign mercenaries," the ministry said.
In addition, some infrastructure facilities of Ukraine’s ports used to receive, store and distribute military cargo, and also fuel and lubricants for the Ukrainian army were degraded, it said.
"During the week, 17 dry cargo ships involved in the delivery of Western weapons, military hardware and equipment for the needs of the Ukrainian army were hit," the ministry reported.
Russia’s Battlegroup North thwarts Ukrainian attempts to break out of encirclement in Kharkov area
Russia’s Battlegroup North thwarted all the Ukrainian army’s attempts during the past week to break out of the encirclement in the northeast of the Kharkov Region, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup North units continue tightening the ring of encirclement of enemy formations in the northeast of the Kharkov Region and expanding the outer area of control. <…> All the enemy’s attempts to break out of the encirclement were thwarted," the ministry said.
Over the week in that area, the enemy lost more than 265 troops, nine armored combat vehicles, six motor vehicles, five all-terrain vehicles and three ground robotic platforms, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup North liberates 352 sq. km since encircling Ukrainian troops in Kharkov area
Russia’s Battlegroup North has liberated 352 sq. km of territory and 20 communities since surrounding Ukrainian armed formations in the northeast of the Kharkov Region, the ministry reported.
"Overall, 352 sq. km of territory and 20 communities have been liberated since the Ukrainian combat group was surrounded in the northeast of the Kharkov Region. Battlegroup North units have destroyed over 1,085 [Ukrainian] troops, 32 armored combat vehicles, 19 motor vehicles, 18 all-terrain vehicles and 31 ground robotic platforms," the ministry said.
Russia’s Battlegroup North inflicts over 2,000 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup North inflicted more than 2,000 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 21 enemy armored combat vehicles in its areas of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
During the past week in the Kharkov and Sumy Regions, Battlegroup North units "inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of six mechanized brigades, two motorized infantry brigades, an airmobile brigade, an unmanned systems brigade, an assault regiment, an unmanned systems regiment of the Ukrainian army, four territorial defense brigades and a National Guard brigade," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 2,000 personnel, 21 armored combat vehicles, 144 motor vehicles, four field artillery guns, two Grad multiple rocket launchers and 11 electronic warfare stations in the areas of responsibility of Russia’s Battlegroup North over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup West inflicts over 1,510 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup West inflicted more than 1,510 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 13 enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
"During the past week, Battlegroup West units gained better lines and positions and inflicted losses on formations of four mechanized brigades, an assault brigade of the Ukrainian army, a marine infantry brigade, a National Guard brigade and two territorial defense brigades," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,510 personnel, 13 armored combat vehicles, 86 motor vehicles, nine field artillery guns and five electronic warfare stations in that frontline area over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup South inflicts over 1,360 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup South inflicted more than 1,360 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed nine enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
"Over the past week, Battlegroup South units improved their forward positions and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of five mechanized brigades, a motorized infantry brigade, an assault brigade, a mountain assault brigade, two airmobile brigades, an unmanned systems brigade, an assault regiment of the Ukrainian army and two marine infantry brigades," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,360 personnel, nine armored combat vehicles, 164 motor vehicles and 10 field artillery guns in that frontline area over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Center advancing in Dobropolye in Donetsk region
Russia’s Battlegroup Center units are advancing in the western and eastern parts of Dobropolye in the Donetsk People’s Republic and keep tightening the ring of encirclement of Ukrainian armed formations in that area, the ministry reported.
"In Dobropolye in the Donetsk People’s Republic, units of the 51st Army are developing an offensive in converging directions in the town’s western and eastern parts and continue tightening the ring of encirclement of formations from the 425th assault regiment of the Ukrainian army, the 4th and 15th National Guard brigades. All the enemy’s attempts to break out of the encirclement or rotate troops have been thwarted," the ministry said.
Russia’s Battlegroup Center forces have eliminated over 375 enemy personnel and two pickup trucks since surrounding Ukrainian troops in Dobropolye in the Donetsk People’s Republic, it said.
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicts over 3,125 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicted more than 3,125 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 17 enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
Over the past week, Battlegroup Center units "inflicted losses on formations of five mechanized brigades, a jaeger brigade, an unmanned systems brigade of the Ukrainian army, a marine infantry brigade and four National Guard brigades," the ministry said.
Overall, the Ukrainian army lost more than 3,125 personnel, 17 armored combat vehicles, 74 motor vehicles, seven field artillery guns and eight electronic warfare stations in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup Center over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicts over 1,740 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicted more than 1,740 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 13 enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
During the week, Battlegroup East units "inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of a mechanized brigade, an airmobile brigade, three air assault brigades, two assault regiments of the Ukrainian army and a marine infantry brigade," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,740 personnel, 13 armored combat vehicles, 55 motor vehicles and five field artillery guns in that frontline area over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminates 220 Ukrainian troops in week
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminated roughly 220 Ukrainian troops and destroyed an enemy armored combat vehicle in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
"Last week, Battlegroup Dnepr units improved their tactical position and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of two mechanized brigades, a mountain assault brigade, an assault regiment of the Ukrainian army and a territorial defense brigade," the ministry said.
"As many as 220 [Ukrainian] military personnel, an armored combat vehicle, 74 motor vehicles, an artillery gun and seven electronic warfare stations were destroyed," it said.
Russian air defenses intercept 5,031 Ukrainian UAVs, four cruise missiles over week
Russian air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 5,031 Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and four Flamingo cruise missiles over the week, the ministry reported.
"Air defense capabilities shot down 37 guided aerial bombs, four rockets of the US-made HIMARS multiple launch rocket system, four Flamingo long-range cruise missiles and 5,031 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the ministry said.
Tally of Ukrainian army’s losses
Overall, the Russian Armed Forces have destroyed 674 Ukrainian combat aircraft, 284 helicopters, 250,151 unmanned aerial vehicles, 672 surface-to-air missile systems, 31,096 tanks and other armored combat vehicles, 1,784 multiple rocket launchers, 36,607 field artillery guns and mortars and 73,407 special military motor vehicles since the start of the special military operation, the ministry reported.

articles.title: Zelensky: Putin’s Goal Is Not Donbas but All of Ukraine
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Russian President Vladimir Putin’s latest rhetoric shows the Kremlin’s ambitions extend far beyond Donbas, as Moscow seeks control over all of Ukraine and the restoration of Soviet-era influence across Russia’s neighborhood.
Speaking remotely at the fifth annual Helsinki Security Forum on Friday, Zelensky cited Putin’s own rhetoric to challenge European skeptics and the idea of neutral mediation.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“So his goal is not the east of Ukraine. It is not Donbas. His aim is to occupy our entire state,” Zelensky said.
Pointing to remarks Putin made at Russia’s Valdai Forum a day earlier, the president argued that the Kremlin’s objectives extend far beyond eastern Ukraine.
“An independent Ukraine, a strong Ukraine, is a big problem for Putin,” Zelensky said.
He highlighted Putin’s assertion that Ukraine cannot exist independently and that other states are supposedly using Ukrainians to wage war against Russia.
“There were important signals yesterday,” he said. “I don’t think he said it accidentally: ‘Ukraine is not a state, and it is not an independent state.’”
Zelensky linked Putin’s latest rhetoric directly to the Russian leader’s long-running fixation on the collapse of the Soviet Union.
He recalled Putin’s infamous 2005 declaration that the fall of the Soviet Union was the greatest geopolitical catastrophe of the 20th century, contrasting that political grievance with the actual human tragedies of the era.
Sandu: Russia Will Remain Major Threat to Europe Even After Ukraine War Ends
“He did not speak about the First World War as a tragedy. He did not recognize the Second World War as [the greatest tragedy]. He did not mention other wars,” Zelensky said.
“He could have mentioned Afghanistan and other things, or the Chornobyl disaster – a horrible disaster. He mentioned none of the things that were connected to human lives.”
Instead, Zelensky argued, Putin focused entirely on the loss of Soviet power.
“Therefore, his goal is obvious: to bring it all back, to bring the USSR back.”
“The fact that he was saying this again yesterday serves as yet another indication of what he wants – of his attitude toward peace, whether he wants the war to end and, even if he does, at what price.”
Zelensky argued that Moscow seeks to recreate not necessarily the Soviet Union in its former institutional form, but the sphere of influence the Kremlin once exercised across neighboring states.
“Undoubtedly, this is about bringing back the influence of the USSR – or Russia’s influence – but making it comparable with the influence the former USSR once had,” he said.
“He has total influence over Belarus. But I am sure that he wants all of that back.”
Warning for the Baltic states and Russia’s neighbors
Zelensky warned that the implications extend beyond Ukraine.
If Putin’s ambition is to restore Moscow’s former regional dominance, he argued, the Baltic states and other countries sharing borders with Russia would also face pressure.
“Therefore, these challenges would also concern the Baltic states and countries with which Russia shares borders,” Zelensky said.
He urged those in Europe who remain skeptical about the scale of Russia’s ambitions to look directly at Putin’s own words.
“And nobody stops him in these messages,” Zelensky said. “And that is weakness of the world.”
Asked about Ukraine’s biggest EU obstacle, Zelensky answers: ‘Putin’
Zelensky was also asked what he considers the greatest obstacle facing Ukraine as it pursues European Union membership while simultaneously fighting Russia’s full-scale war.
His answer was one word:
“Putin.”
“He really doesn’t want that to happen,” Zelensky said.
“And it’s not about his opinion, but what he’s doing for this not to happen – against the development of our state, against the geopolitical choice of the people.”
“When we are talking about what the EU means for Ukraine, it is a victory over Russia – even a victory over Putin,” he said.
“Because the EU is the choice of our people.”
Security guarantees, he added, are critical because they protect Ukraine’s ability to follow the geopolitical course chosen by its citizens.
“And therefore it is important to have security guarantees, because these guarantees protect the path that the people of Ukraine have chosen.”
The Helsinki Security Forum is being held in the Finnish capital from Oct. 2–4 under the theme “Layers of Security.” The fifth annual gathering brings together policymakers and experts to discuss European defense, technological sovereignty, transatlantic relations, energy security, nuclear deterrence and Russia’s role in European security.
‘You cannot build total defense’ by buying weapons
Zelensky also used the forum to lay out lessons Ukraine has learned after years of defending itself against Russia.
A country seeking genuine security must first develop strength from within, he said, beginning with its military.
“The main guarantee for Ukraine is the army of our state.”
But an experienced army alone is not sufficient, Zelensky argued.
He emphasized the importance of a technologically advanced force, a domestic military-technology sector and defense production capable of rapidly adapting to battlefield requirements.
Energy resilience is another critical component, he said, particularly decentralization of infrastructure vulnerable to attack.
Ukraine shifts from weapons recipient to security partner
The second layer of security, Zelensky said, is international cooperation.
He thanked the EU, European countries and the US for financial, technological and military assistance since the outbreak of the war.
Ukraine received weapons it previously lacked, including NATO-standard systems, he noted, but its relationship with partners is increasingly becoming a two-way exchange.
Ukraine is now sharing knowledge gained through years of high-intensity warfare.
Zelensky highlighted a recent drone cooperation agreement with Finland as an example.
“It’s not about just selling or buying drones or missiles,” he said.
“It’s about sharing your security experience throughout the duration of this agreement.”
Ukraine is willing to share that knowledge with countries that supported it, Zelensky said, pointing to the trust built between Kyiv and Helsinki.
The third layer is collective security, particularly NATO.
Zelensky congratulated Finland on securing guarantees through membership in both the European Union and NATO.
“These are allies in economy, allies in technology, and allies in security,” he said.
“This is of utmost importance, and this is what Ukraine is counting on.”

articles.title: Germany is preparing for war – with an enemy it expects to hold back
articles.body:
Germany is preparing for war – with an enemy it expects to hold back
“What’s good for a Russian is death to a German.” Russian speakers often use this tongue-in-cheek saying to explain the differences between the Russian and German mindsets, whether in everyday matters – such as how mustard should taste – or in deeper questions of worldview and existence.
Many scholars, including the distinguished Russian historian Vasily Klyuchevsky, have attributed this unmistakable civilizational divide between Europe’s two largest peoples to geography, climate, and landscape, which shaped different ways of life. Living in a predictable climate, Germans developed a habit of methodical, steady work. They could plan ahead because their surroundings allowed them to anticipate the results of their efforts with considerable certainty. Russians, by contrast, inhabit a land of unpredictable conditions stretching, in the words of Russia’s modern national anthem, “from the southern seas to the polar frontier.” They have often found that planning ahead can prove utterly futile. As a result, they frequently have to work at a furious pace within tight deadlines, relying on the distinctly Russian notion of avos: the hope that somehow, things will work out.
These cultural differences help explain not only how relations between these near neighbors evolved over the centuries – remember that the Russian city of Kaliningrad was once the German city of Königsberg – but also the internal logic driving Russian-German political relations today.
Germany’s current leadership views Russia as a threat to national security, much as its predecessors did on the eve of the First and Second World Wars. It is methodically remilitarizing the economy and expanding military assistance to Ukraine in an effort to weaken Russia across the board. In 2022-2023, at the beginning of the special military operation, aid packages were limited in scale and narrowly targeted. Starting in 2024, however, Berlin shifted toward long-term contracts for equipment and drones worth more than $10 billion a year, making Germany the EU’s largest provider of bilateral military assistance to Ukraine.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, formerly Germany’s defense minister, has quietly emerged as the chief overseer of how German funds are distributed. Meanwhile, in keeping with this gradual drift toward military confrontation with our country, Friedrich Merz’s government is continuing Olaf Scholz’s policy of dismantling Russia’s diplomatic presence in Germany. After forcing the closure of Russian consulates general in Munich, Hamburg, Frankfurt, and Leipzig in May 2023, Berlin decided this September to shut down the consulate general in Bonn and the Russian House cultural center in Berlin.
With the EU’s largest economy and its own appointee in one of the most powerful positions in Europe’s supranational hierarchy, Berlin is gradually ‘reprogramming’ a united Europe into something resembling a ‘Fourth Reich’. As it becomes a more cohesive center of power, Europe risks finding itself on the brink of military confrontation with its powerful eastern neighbor, as it has repeatedly throughout history. To make the supposed Russian threat seem tangible, German authorities have been feeding the media rumors since this summer about Moscow’s involvement in the discovery of an explosives-laden drone at Leipzig’s cargo airport. Without waiting for the investigation’s final findings, Berlin rushed to accuse Russia of orchestrating an act of sabotage.
Recognizing that their government has set the country on a dead-end course, ordinary German citizens are beginning to push back, increasingly throwing their support behind Alternative for Germany (AfD). The party promises a 180-degree turn in both foreign and domestic policy – not a “360-degree” turn, as former Foreign Minister Annalena Baerbock once proposed, inadvertently producing Germany’s defining political meme of the past decade. In the 2021 election, the main opposition party won just 10% of the vote. Four years later, in the snap election of 2025, its share reached 28.5%. For the first time since German reunification in 1990, it came out on top in every eastern state of the former East Germany. This year, AfD consolidated its gains with victories in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
To be sure, the party’s victories remain regional, and Germany’s other political parties refuse to consider the movement led by Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla even as a hypothetical coalition partner. But if its electoral base continues to expand, drawing support not only from native-born Germans but eventually from immigrant communities as well, AfD could have a chance of securing more than 50% of the vote nationwide. That would allow it to form a government on its own.
Meanwhile, Merz’s personal approval rating has fallen to an all-time low for a chancellor in the history of the Federal Republic: just 11-15%, with 85–89% dissatisfied. Facing those numbers and recognizing public demand for a more balanced relationship with Russia, he instructed Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul to secure a meeting with his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, whatever it took. Lavrov’s account makes clear just how little substance that encounter contained:
”As for German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, he requested a meeting at the last minute. We had an opening this morning, before my address to the General Assembly. We never refuse to hear out any of our colleagues, including those who accuse Russia of every sin imaginable… When we met, I invited Foreign Minister Wadephul to explain what he had come to discuss. He took out his notes and read a text that repeated, word for word, what Germany’s leaders say publicly and officially every day. I told him as much. I learned nothing new… I told him frankly that I had thought he might have something interesting or out of the ordinary to say. They could simply have called and told us to read their official statements…”
Why have relations between Moscow and Berlin deteriorated so profoundly that even meetings between their foreign ministers have become fruitless exchanges of prepared talking points, rather than negotiations aimed at a breakthrough? At least three factors deserve attention.
1) Berlin’s unconstructive role in efforts to resolve the conflict in Ukraine
From the earliest days of the Ukraine crisis, Germany sought to control the diplomatic process in order to put the country firmly on an anti-Russian course. In February 2014, after unrest broke out on the Maidan, Foreign Minister Frank-Walter Steinmeier and his French and Polish counterparts, Laurent Fabius and Radoslaw Sikorski, acted as guarantors of an agreement between President Viktor Yanukovich and the opposition. It called for a national unity government, early elections, and an end to all forms of violence. As we know, the protesters soon violated the agreement, took up arms, and staged the ‘Revolution of Dignity’.
A year later, German Chancellor Angela Merkel and French President François Hollande joined Russia as mediators in talks between Kiev and the Donetsk and Lugansk People’s Republics, culminating in the signing of the package of measures to implement the Minsk agreements. After leaving office, Merkel admitted that Minsk II had been needed not to end Ukraine’s civil war, but to provide cover for further arming the Ukrainian military.
Is it any wonder, then, that Russian diplomats prefer talks without European mediators who have discredited themselves? Or that Moscow sees proposals such as an ‘energy truce’ or a ‘Black Sea initiative’ as diplomatic support for the military campaign in the special operation zone, rather than sincere attempts to resolve the conflict? Their purpose is to supply Ukraine with the manpower and resources needed to inflict the ‘strategic defeat’ on Russia that has become a mantra among European politicians.
2) The severing of trade and economic ties with Russia
Apart from brief recessions associated with global upheavals such as the financial crisis of 2008-2009 and the COVID-19 pandemic of 2020-2021, Germany’s economy recorded steady annual growth of 1-3.5% in the 21st century. Cheap Russian energy, which helped fuel industrial expansion, was one of the most important ingredients in that success. Another was access to Russia’s sizable market, where more than 6,000 German companies were doing business at the peak of commercial ties.
Germany’s modern ‘economic miracle’ came to an end when its government became a driving force behind the EU’s adoption of a 21st sanctions package, prompting a mass exodus of German capital from Russia. Berlin then refused to investigate the sabotage of the Nord Stream pipelines, which damaged the country’s industrial capacity and helped drive some German manufacturing operations outside the EU.
As a result, the economy has stagnated since 2022, with an annual shortfall of around 1%. The broader social and political climate offers little cause for optimism, as low birth rates and an influx of illegal immigrants put growing pressure on public finances. All of this invites grim thoughts about the inevitability of Germany’s “self-destruction,” to borrow the term used by German commentator Thilo Sarrazin. At least, that is, Germany as it has existed since reunification – a process that essentially amounted to West Germany economically ‘devouring’ the East, an approach that reached its natural limits in the early 2020s.
3) Confidence that Russia will act responsibly
Russia has long served as a bogeyman in the German media. Yet, paradoxically, Germany’s government is militarizing the economy in the belief that an actual shooting war may never materialize.
First, the longer Germany uses Ukraine as a military and political battering ram against Russia, the longer Russian forces will remain focused on the special military operation. That spares Germany’s regular armed forces from having to fight Russia directly with everything at their disposal.
Second, as a responsible member of the nuclear club, Russia has repeatedly stated that it will use nuclear weapons only if the very existence of the state is at stake. This allows Berlin and other European ‘warmongers’ to keep the fighting conventional and geographically confined to the former Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic, avoiding any need to discover firsthand how far Russia’s resolve extends.
Finally, however belligerent some German politicians may sound, they cannot simply switch off their historical memory. It reminds them that over the past three centuries alone, the Russian army has liberated Berlin – Germany’s present-day capital – three times, exactly once per century. It is hard to imagine a German politician today eager to play ‘Russian roulette’ a fourth time. And that brings us back to a defining difference between Russians and Germans: we may take a long time to harness the horses, but once we get moving, we move fast – especially in times of great geopolitical upheaval.

articles.title: Ukraine Tests Five High-Speed Drone Interceptor Models to Counter Russia’s Jet-Powered Attacks
articles.body:
Ukraine is testing five high-speed interceptor drone models designed to shoot down Russia’s increasingly common jet-powered attack drones, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview with the Financial Times published Friday.
One of the five models could reach production of around 400 units by the end of October, while the other four remain under testing, Zelensky said.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Jet-powered drones, which blur the line between drones and missiles, have been increasingly used by Russia against Ukraine in recent attacks, posing challenges for Ukrainian air defenses as current interceptor drones struggle to catch up with their higher speeds.
Zelensky said Russia launched around 500 drones against Ukraine in a recent 24-hour period, about half of them jet-powered. Ukraine is currently destroying about 57% of the jet-powered drones, compared with 85% to 90% of conventional drones, he told the FT.
The faster drones have created a new challenge for Ukraine’s layered air defenses. Reuters reported in September that some Ukrainian interceptor prototypes struggled to remain controllable at speeds exceeding 400 kilometers per hour during testing, showing the technical difficulty of developing drones capable of chasing and destroying the new Russian weapons.
Ukrainian manufacturers have nevertheless begun developing interceptors specifically for the threat. One model unveiled in September, the Zorelit v5, has a reported top speed of 416 kilometers per hour and a range of up to 47 kilometers.
Kyiv Grinds to a Halt as Russian Strikes Shut Bridges, Force People to Walk
Its manufacturer says it can be used against both conventional Shahed-type drones and faster jet-powered variants.
The biggest obstacle to rapidly scaling production is not only technology but supply.
“Engines are key,” Zelensky told the FT. “We really import a lot of engines.” He said Ukraine produces some engines domestically but does not have enough to meet demand. He also cited a shortage of budget funding for the development and mass production of air-defense weapons.
Ukraine has been working to expand domestic production of the technology. Zelensky said last week that new decisions had been made to establish production of several types of jet engines inside Ukraine, following tests of interceptor drones against Russian jet-powered Shaheds.
The interceptor program has become increasingly urgent as Russia intensifies its aerial campaign against Ukrainian cities ahead of winter.
The new interceptor drones are intended to provide Ukraine with a cheaper and more scalable layer of air defense against the faster weapons, reducing pressure on scarce surface-to-air missiles and fighter jets.
Zelensky said US-made F-16s have proved effective against the new Russian drones, but argued that too many Ukrainian aircraft are undergoing lengthy maintenance in Europe. Kyiv wants more repair work moved inside Ukraine so the fighters can return to service faster.
What changed in Russia’s drone war in Ukraine?
Since Aug. 27, Kyiv has been living under a near-continuous drone campaign.
Russia shifted its long-range drone tactics that day, replacing the large swarms once or twice a week that Kyiv residents had become accustomed to with repeated waves across Ukrainian airspace.
The change was particularly noticeable in the capital, where attacks have increasingly continued into daytime hours.
As of Friday, Oct. 2, there has been no clear let-up. Repeated drone attacks have disrupted life in Kyiv, while strikes on warehouses, businesses and other civilian infrastructure have increasingly affected economic activity.
Russia has also sharply increased its use of jet-powered drones.
Ukrainian Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said Russia launched 3,177 jet-powered UAVs in September as of Sept. 29, compared with 2,850 drones of all types in August.
“We have already had more drones this month than in the previous month overall,” Ihnat said, adding that Russian forces were continuing to attack in waves.
Kyiv and the Kyiv region remained the main focus, he said, while Kharkiv, Odesa, Mykolaiv, Sumy, Kherson and Dnipro were also repeatedly targeted.
The increase marks a dramatic escalation from earlier in the summer. Ihnat previously said Russia used about 350 jet-powered drones in June, 1,500 in July and 2,850 in August.
The new drones are significantly faster than the older piston-engine Shahed variants, making them harder for Ukraine’s existing low-cost interceptors to catch.

articles.title: Russia Plans Up to 1,000 Strikes to Cripple Ukraine’s Energy Grid This Winter
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Plans Up to 1,000 Strikes to Cripple Ukraine’s Energy Grid This Winter
Russia is preparing what Ukrainian officials describe as its most ambitious campaign yet to cripple Ukraine’s power, heating, and water systems this winter, The New York Times reported on October 2.
The assessment is based on a document Ukrainian Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal recently presented to European partners in Paris. Two people familiar with the briefing told The New York Times that Shmyhal described it as an intercepted Russian plan for a methodical campaign against Ukraine’s energy system.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Last winter, Russian missile and drone strikes repeatedly targeted Ukraine’s energy and civilian infrastructure, leaving large parts of Kyiv without electricity, heating, and water in subzero temperatures. UNITED24 Media reported that one January attack alone left more than 1 million people without power and over 4,000 apartment buildings without heat.
According to the document obtained by The New York Times, Russia could use up to 1,000 missiles, drones, and guided bombs against electrical substations, hydroelectric and thermal power plants, boiler houses, and other infrastructure.
The plan also envisages attacks on electrical switchyards connecting Ukraine’s three operating nuclear power plants to the national grid. The facilities are located less than a mile from the reactors, The New York Times noted.
By striking those switchyards, Russia would seek to force the nuclear plants offline without directly attacking the reactors themselves.
The document also describes attacks on Ukraine’s water infrastructure, including pumping stations and wastewater treatment plants, using dozens of ballistic missiles and guided bombs. The New York Times wrote that Russia has not previously targeted such facilities on that scale.
Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa are identified as priority targets. The document outlines plans to reduce electricity and heating supplies in those cities by as much as 90% while severely disrupting sewage systems.
The New York Times could not independently authenticate the document, which is dated August and written in Russian. However, the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, has publicly threatened an expanded campaign against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure this winter.
“Our partners, like us, were struck by its cynicism, by this cold, terrorist calculation of how to destroy our energy sector,” Shmyhal stated previously when discussing the document publicly.
The apparent plan is divided into three stages, The New York Times reported. The first would target substations near Ukraine’s western border that allow the country to import electricity from Europe.
The second stage would focus on hydroelectric power plants, while the third would attempt to disconnect Ukraine’s three operating nuclear power plants from the grid. The document estimates that the campaign could eliminate nearly 15 gigawatts of generating capacity.
Ukraine has spent recent months strengthening critical infrastructure, repairing power plants and substations, and installing smaller distributed energy facilities that are harder to destroy. Authorities have also reinforced parts of the grid to reroute electricity when transmission infrastructure is damaged.
Those preparations remain vulnerable to renewed attacks. Energy analyst Maria Tsaturian told The New York Times that only a small number of major strikes could eliminate much of the five gigawatts of generating capacity Ukraine restored in recent months.
Russia has already begun renewed attacks on energy infrastructure ahead of winter. Before dawn on September 30, missiles and drones struck a major thermal power plant and other facilities, leaving parts of Kyiv without electricity and water, The New York Times reported.
Ukraine endured prolonged outages during the previous winter as Russian attacks repeatedly damaged power and heating facilities. In Kyiv, residents sometimes went 12 hours or more without electricity, while outages also disrupted water supplies, elevators, and heating systems in apartment buildings.
UNITED24 Media previously reported that Kyiv was stockpiling emergency food and drinking water ahead of the 2026–2027 winter, preparing for possible prolonged blackouts caused by renewed Russian strikes on energy infrastructure. The city also planned to expand emergency food reserves and support Points of Invincibility during extended outages.

articles.title: Russia planning to increase "hybrid warfare" activity in Europe, Ukrainian intelligence warns
articles.body:
Russia planning to increase 'hybrid warfare' activity in Europe, Ukrainian intelligence warns
Russia's secret services have been tasked with increasing the number of attacks in Europe, Ukrainian military intelligence (HUR) warned in a statement on Oct. 2.
"The special services of the aggressor state of Russia have been tasked with increasing activity on the territory of the European Union and NATO states — this involves preparing for hybrid operations aimed at undermining aid to Ukraine and weakening the Alliance's capabilities," the statement says.
Acts of Russian "hybrid warfare" have included arson, assassinations, and a recent attempt to blow up Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft with modified FPV drones in Leipzig in August. On Sept. 1, Germany formally accused Russia of carrying out the attack.
"To carry out operations, including sabotage operations, the Kremlin plans to involve agents recruited by the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces (GRU) and the FSB of the Russian Federation in Europe. The Russian special services are targeting military facilities, critical infrastructure, and communication systems," the statement says.
"Among the aggressor's likely targets are Starlink satellite internet receiving stations located in European countries," HUR said.
Starlink, manufactured and operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX, is widely used for communications by the Ukrainian military.
On Sept. 24, Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski told reporters that a fire at a Starlink ground station in Poland may have been a deliberate attempt to disrupt internet access used by Ukrainian forces at the front.
Gawkowski said there were indications that the fire at the station in Wola Krobowska, in Poland's Masovian Voivodeship, on the evening of Sept. 23, may have been an attempt to disrupt its operations.
The station is operated by the state-owned telecommunications company Exatel and serves as an internet hub that carries traffic through Poland, including to Ukraine, Gawkowski said.
He suggested Russia could be behind the incident, describing it as potentially part of Moscow's hybrid warfare. Polish authorities have not concluded their investigation into the incident.
European governments are stepping up preparations for possible Russian hybrid attacks as officials across the continent warn that Moscow could increasingly use drones, missiles, sabotage, and cyberattacks to test NATO countries and pressure them over their support for Ukraine.
"The Ukrainian Defense Ministry's Directorate of Defense warned its partners about the criminal plans of the aggressor state of Russia," the statement says.

articles.title: Mirage 2000 Makes History—Russian Banderol Cruise Missile Shot Down With Guns
articles.body:

Mirage 2000 Makes History—Russian Banderol Cruise Missile Shot Down With Guns
A Ukrainian Mirage 2000-5F has reportedly scored a first, shooting down a Russian S8000 Banderol cruise missile not with an air-to-air missile, but with bursts from its built-in 30mm cannons.
“Late-night information: the Mirage 2000-5F was the first Western fighter aircraft to destroy a Russian S8000 Banderol cruise missile with the cannon,” according to Militarnyi, citing OSINT analyst French Aid to Europe on October 2.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The claim has not yet been publicly confirmed by the Ukrainian or French defense ministries.
France transferred Mirage 2000-5F fighters from its own Air and Space Force inventory to Ukraine beginning in 2025, giving Kyiv another Western fighter type for air-defense and strike missions.
The aircraft is particularly well suited to interception work. France describes the 2000-5F as an air-defense-focused variant equipped with an RDY multimode radar, MICA air-to-air missiles and two internal 30mm cannons.
Those guns are DEFA 554 revolver cannons mounted inside the fuselage. Each carries roughly 125 rounds and can fire at rates reaching about 1,800 rounds per minute, giving the pilot an extremely short but intense window of fire during a close-range interception.
If confirmed, the engagement would be particularly notable because the target was not a slow propeller-driven Shahed.
The S8000 Banderol is a small Russian jet-powered cruise missile developed by Kronstadt JSC. Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence lists its top speed at roughly 620–650 kilometers per hour, with a cruising speed of 520–560 km/h and a range of around 500 kilometers.
The weapon is primarily launched from Russia’s Orion UAV and is also being adapted for use from Mi-28N attack helicopters. It combines relatively low production cost with the speed and flight characteristics of a small cruise missile, making it a more difficult interception target than conventional Shahed-type drones.
The Banderol carries a large high-explosive fragmentation warhead and has increasingly appeared in Russian attacks against Ukraine since its first documented combat use in spring 2025. Ukrainian intelligence says the weapon relies on numerous foreign-made components, including its propulsion and electronics.
Earlier, two Mirage 2000 fighter jets crewed by French and Ukrainian pilots participated in France’s Bastille Day military parade on July 14, with one aircraft expected to appear in the colors of the Ukrainian flag.

articles.title: Trump talking his own imagination about Iran
articles.body:
Trump talking his own imagination about Iran
TEHRAN – Trump has claimed that Iran would have “wiped” Israel and Saudi Arabia “off the face of the planet” with nuclear bombs if he had not been president.
Modern history may not have seen a statesman as fabulist as Trump. He seems to be losing his sense of reality more and more as the midterm congressional elections approach.
Trump is living in a world of his own imagination, indulging in his own fantasies. It is in this imaginary world that Iran would have developed nuclear weapons and destroyed Israel, Saudi Arabia and many other countries if he had not been president.
“If I weren't president, Saudi Arabia wouldn't be here right now. Neither would Israel. They'd be wiped off the face of the planet. I do a lot for Saudi Arabia. My relationship with them is very good. I like the crown prince. My relationship is very good. But remember, if I weren't here, there wouldn't be a Saudi Arabia. There wouldn't be an Israel. There wouldn't be various other countries also,” Trump told the Time magazine in an interview published on October 1.
According to such a statement, Iran gained access to nuclear arms in Trump’s world of imagination and dropped atomic weapons on Israel and Saudi Arabia and wiped them out.
It is open to all that Trump is the laughing stock of the world.
Even Israeli hardliners who have been seeking hard to demonize Iran laugh about such remarks from the bottom of their heart.
In August 2016, former French President François Hollande made a statement about Trump that history will not forget. At the time, when Trump was running for the White House, Hollande said that Trump's “excesses end up making you feel like you want to retch.”
The way Trump speaks is degrading for a top official, let alone that the official be the president of the United States. His remarks and approach to domestic and foreign policy is extremely reckless and shameful.
Even the far-right government of Netanyahu, whose barbarity against Gazans has shocked the world, suspended Heritage Minister Amihay Eliyahu in November 2023 who suggested dropping nuclear bomb on Gaza.
Unfortunately, Trump is surrounded by sycophants. There is no unbiased official in his inner circle to advise him against making such ridiculous remarks.
Trump cannot fool anyone with such ridiculous remarks if he is referring to Iran’s strikes on U.S. military bases in the Persian Gulf Arab states that were used as launchpads for the U.S. war against Iran. Iran had repeatedly and unequivocally announced that it would target any location from which an attack was launched against it. Who could expect Iran to come under attack from a military base in a regional country and not strike that base?
Confusing Iran’s retaliatory defensive strikes on military bases from which U.S. fighter jets flew to drop bombs on Iran with the fantasy that Iran would have used nuclear weapons to “wipe off the face of the planet” Saudi Arabia and “various other countries” if Trump had not attacked Iran is not only laughable but also a distortion of the realities on the ground.
Iran also fired missiles at Israel, which, along with the United States, launched joint aggression against Iran in both June 2025 and February 2026. Even before the full-scale wars of 2025 and 2026, it was Israel that launched attacks on Iran’s diplomatic headquarters in Damascus and carried out assassinations inside Iran, forcing Tehran to respond.
Trump is seeking to sell his imagined narrative to the American people and others around the world in a futile attempt to justify his ill-gotten war against Iran and portray the country as a demon. In doing so, however, he risks making himself appear even more ridiculous.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia preparing massive Yemen offensive – Reuters
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia preparing massive Yemen offensive – Reuters
Saudi Arabia is planning a major offensive in civil war-torn Yemen, hoping to reverse gains made by the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels, who seized a strategic Red Sea chokepoint last month, Reuters reported on Friday, citing Gulf and Yemeni officials and Western diplomats.
More than 100,000 Yemeni government troops could be mobilized for the offensive, depending on the scale, according to Reuters. The operation would be overseen by Saudi Arabia and supported by Saudi airstrikes. The US and other Western countries providing intelligence and material support to Riyadh are not expected to take part in combat operations.
According to Reuters, the Saudis are considering two options: an attack focused on recapturing the coastal area around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, or a broader offensive involving synchronized attacks on multiple fronts in Al-Bayda, Marib, Taiz, and Al-Jawf.
Saudi Arabia first intervened in Yemen in 2015 to support the internationally recognized government, which the Houthis had driven from the capital, Sanaa, the previous year. Large-scale fighting decreased significantly following a UN-brokered truce in 2022.
The fighting escalated again last month, with the Houthis accusing Riyadh of imposing an illegal siege on Yemen. The rebels have since captured the strategic port of Mokha and Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The Houthis said on Friday that Saudi forces carried out 94 strikes on areas under their control over the previous 24 hours. Omar al-Bukhaiti, a spokesman for the Houthi-run government in Sanaa, accused the kingdom of deliberately targeting civilian sites, including schools and health facilities.
The group earlier fired drones and missiles at Saudi Arabia, targeting energy facilities, but denied striking a power station in Medina, one of Islam’s holiest cities, dismissing the Saudi claim as a “lie.”
The escalation in Yemen comes amid the ongoing US-Iran war, with the Strait of Hormuz remaining closed to most shipping and US-Iranian talks on ending the conflict stalled.
Several Saudi allies have stepped up military support for the kingdom. Britain has agreed to provide air-to-air refueling for Saudi warplanes, while France is sending troops, radar, and air-defense systems to help protect the Red Sea oil hub of Yanbu.
Pakistan has deployed 30,000 to 40,000 troops to Saudi Arabia to help defend its borders and intercept missiles and drones, Reuters reported, citing a Pakistani official. Islamabad has also supplied air-defense systems, artillery, drones, and anti-drone equipment, while Pakistani military advisers are working alongside Saudi personnel supporting Yemeni forces. Pakistan has not, however, decided to send troops into Yemen for combat operations.

articles.title: Poland Drafts New “Prewar” Defense Law to Speed Up Allied Troop Deployments

Poland Drafts New “Prewar” Defense Law to Speed Up Allied Troop Deployments
Poland’s Defense Ministry is drafting a new law to prepare the state for a possible prewar period, including earlier troop deployments and stronger coordination between civilian authorities and the military, Rzeczpospolita reported on October 2.
The proposed legislation would create a clearer legal framework for moving from peacetime readiness toward full defense readiness before martial law is formally introduced. It would also allow earlier deployment of Polish and allied forces to strategically important areas, Rzeczpospolita wrote.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Poland’s efforts to strengthen defense readiness come amid repeated Russian aerial threats near its eastern border. Days earlier, a Russian jet-powered drone crashed near the Yahodyn checkpoint on Ukraine’s border with Poland, prompting Warsaw to scramble fighter jets and place air defense and radar units on heightened readiness.
Poland’s Defense Ministry confirmed to Rzeczpospolita that the draft is intended to strengthen national defense capabilities and improve cooperation between the armed forces and agencies responsible for internal security.
The ministry stated that the legislation is designed to adapt Poland’s legal framework to “modern threats, in particular those of a hybrid, cyber, and disinformation nature.”
According to Rzeczpospolita, the law would also link Poland’s Defense Response Plan more closely with NATO’s Response System and expand preparations for military infrastructure and logistics. It would broaden the number of institutions involved in permanent duty systems and clarify responsibilities across public administration.
The legislation is also intended to improve planning outside the military sphere, change rules governing defense training and exercises, and prepare civilian institutions to carry out defense tasks under both permanent and full defense readiness.
Poland currently operates under two levels of defense readiness introduced in March 2025, Rzeczpospolita noted. Permanent readiness applies during peacetime, while full defense readiness can be introduced in the event of an external security threat or war and allows mobilization and the full deployment of the state’s defense system.
“Due to the complex legislative process, it is currently unknown when the bill will be submitted to the Sejm for consideration,” the Defense Ministry told Rzeczpospolita.
A similar proposal was prepared in 2023 under then-President Andrzej Duda, but it did not enter into force. Rzeczpospolita reported that some of its provisions were later incorporated into government regulations.
Poland had previously simplified its military procedures for identifying and shooting down foreign objects entering national airspace. The new rules allow Polish forces to act on radar, surveillance, and Ukrainian data without first requiring visual confirmation, giving air defenses more time to respond during Russian drone and missile attacks near the border.

articles.title: Russia May Use Mesh Relays in Kyiv to Steer Drones, Adviser Says
articles.body:
Russian forces may be deploying ground-based Mesh-network repeaters inside Kyiv to establish real-time remote control over Shahed strike drones and adjust flight vectors during attacks, Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to the Ukrainian presidency on defense technology, stated on Saturday, Oct. 3.
Writing on Facebook, Beskrestnov, a communications specialist known by the callsign “Flash,” explained that clandestine signal repeaters situated within the capital could create temporary communication links enabling Russian operators to actively pilot loitering munitions onto high-value targets.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Beskrestnov estimated that between one and three such covert repeaters could currently be operating in the metropolitan area.
“Such repeaters are difficult to find, but we must search for them,” Beskrestnov said. “As long as they exist, shielding the city with electronic warfare will not be effective.”
Beskrestnov noted that while the deployment of ground repeaters represents an unconfirmed hypothesis, the technical anomaly demands rigorous investigation.
He pointed out that technical specialists continue to examine the wreckage of downed Russian drones and have yet to discover onboard communication modules that would definitively confirm real-time manual piloting.
Electronic warfare vulnerabilities
Beskrestnov cited recent precision strikes against Kyiv’s transit bridges and air defense positions as operational indicators suggesting that Russian loitering munitions may possess real-time guidance capabilities beyond preset satellite coordinates.
Russia Threatens to Strike Defense Plants in NATO Countries
The technology adviser highlighted that Russian military channels have extensively circulated photographs and visual intelligence of Ukrainian air defense assets deployed along capital bridges, including German-supplied Gepard self-propelled anti-aircraft guns.
“Informationally, it is impossible to hide a Gepard on a bridge from the adversary when tens of thousands of people cross it daily,” Beskrestnov explained. “Why do I mention this? As long as online control of Shaheds exists, not only bridges will be targeted, but also air defense assets themselves.”
Beskrestnov stated that his technical analysis evaluated previous drone strikes against Dnipro River bridges alongside the mathematical feasibility of Russian forces maintaining long-range Mesh communication links directly from Russian border territory.
The adviser noted that if localized ground repeaters bypass electronic warfare jamming shields, mobile air defense gun crews face acute counter-battery risks from loitering munitions capable of terminal course correction.
The Volodymyrska Street SBU headquarters strike
As a primary operational case study supporting the ground-repeater hypothesis, Beskrestnov cited the Sept. 4 drone strike against the central headquarters of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) in central Kyiv.
According to technical tracking of that incident, no secondary Russian drones were airborne in the capital area during the strike that could have functioned as aerial signal retransmission nodes, suggesting that any manual flight adjustments would have required an alternative, ground-level signal conduit.
The Sept. 4 attack directly targeted the central SBU administration building situated on Volodymyrska Street in Kyiv’s historic Shevchenkivskyi district, across from the UNESCO World Heritage site of St. Sophia Cathedral.
President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed at the time that the incoming loitering munition was directed specifically at the office of SBU Chief Oleksandr Poklad.
The strike on the intelligence headquarters injured seven people, hospitalizing six, while causing localized structural fires and shattering masonry across adjacent commercial buildings, including the Zavertaylo restaurant near the Zoloti Vorota metro station.

articles.title: New Ukrainian ballistic missile used in combat
articles.body:
Ukraine has used a domestically built tactical ballistic missile in combat for the first time, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said, naming the weapon as the FP-7 and signalling that the next task is building it in quantity, according to the president in a post published on Thursday.
Writing on X, Mr Zelensky said: “Ukrainian tactical ballistic missile. FP-7. First combat use. Thank you for the result. Next up: production. Glory to Ukraine!”
No target was given, and Kyiv has declined to say what the missile struck. The brevity of the announcement is itself the point, since a first combat firing is a political statement about Ukrainian industry as much as a military event.
Ukrainian tactical ballistic missile. FP-7. First combat use. Thank you for the result. Next up: production. Glory to Ukraine! pic.twitter.com/IxdjVg51c1
— Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) October 1, 2026
The FP-7 is made by Fire Point, the Ukrainian company set up in 2022 that has become one of the more visible names in the country’s wartime weapons industry, and which also produces the FP-1 one-way attack drone and the FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile. The missile is launched from a standard truck trailer rather than a purpose-built transporter erector launcher, an approach that keeps cost down and makes the launch vehicle harder to distinguish from ordinary traffic.
Published figures for the missile vary between sources and none of them have been independently verified. The announced range has been given as between 200 and 300 kilometres, with a warhead variously described as 150 or 200 kilograms, a circular error probable of around 14 metres and a terminal velocity of 1,200 to 1,500 metres a second. Analysts tracking the programme have assessed that the airframe derives from the Soviet 48N6 interceptor used by the S-400 system, rebuilt with composite materials and modern electronics, and the manufacturer has claimed that the resulting speed gives it a better chance of getting through air defences than the Russian Iskander.
Roughly seven months separated the first reported test from this firing, which is fast by any peacetime standard and reflects how much Ukrainian procurement has compressed since 2022.

Ukraine’s Acoustic SkyFortress Will Track Low-Flying Drones and Missiles Over Lithuania
Lithuania is deploying the Ukrainian-developed SkyFortress system to test acoustic and radio-frequency detection of low-flying drones and cruise missiles, the country’s Defense Ministry announced on October 2.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Lithuanian Defense Ministry reported that SkyFortress will operate as an experimental airspace surveillance system capable of identifying objects by their acoustic or electromagnetic signatures. The system uses artificial intelligence to classify and track detected threats in real time.
“Instead of developing everything from scratch, we are adapting systems that are already operating in Ukraine,” Lithuanian Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas stated.
“SkyFortress complements the first stage of this chain—surveillance: with the help of artificial intelligence, the system detects and tracks low-flying drones or cruise missiles.”
Under an agreement signed this summer, the deployment includes processing sensor-collected data, using libraries of acoustic and radio-frequency digital signatures based on unclassified information, and training Lithuanian personnel.
Testing will assess SkyFortress’ ability to detect and identify low-flying unmanned aircraft under Lithuanian conditions.
Earlier in September, Lithuania itself confronted the challenge directly when NATO fighter jets shot down an unidentified drone that had entered Lithuanian airspace from Belarus, highlighting the urgency of enhanced detection capabilities across the Baltic region.

articles.title: ‘The enemy is tearing our city apart’: terror in Kyiv as Russia ramps up attacks
articles.body:
Valeriya Tkachenko was dropping her son off at school in central Kyiv when the air raid alert sounded. Staff hurried the children and parents into the shelter, where the frightened lawyer spent the next two hours with her son.
“I’m scared to death all day about what could happen to my son,” she said as she emerged from the shelter, already late for work.
A day earlier, a Russian jet-powered drone had struck a school nearby. “And I can’t plan anything any more,” she said. “It’s not sustainable like this.”
Across the city on Friday morning, Artem Marchenko, an IT worker, was forced to abandon his car and walk for 20 minutes across the Pivdennyi, or Southern, Bridge on his way to work after repeated Russian strikes damaged the crossing.
He feared Russia would soon target Kyiv’s other bridges, paralysing movement across a city of about 3 million people, the two halves of which are divided by the Dnipro.
On Saturday morning, Russia targeted a second major bridge connecting Kyiv, damaging the road surface on the Northern Bridge and temporarily halting traffic.
Kyiv is entering its most difficult period since the early days of the invasion, as intensifying Russian attacks reshape everyday life in a capital that Moscow is seeking to plunge into darkness.
For weeks, the main worry in the capital had been the coming winter, when Russia is expected once again to try to plunge Ukraine into darkness and cold. But a sharp escalation in Russian attacks has left many residents feeling that some of the hardship they had been bracing for is already here.
“The capital is in a very dramatic situation. And it’s no longer possible to pretend that we can live now as we do in peacetime,” the Kyiv mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said on Friday. “The enemy is tearing Kyiv apart.”
This week alone, Russian missiles and drones have struck offices, datacentres, a school and hospital and one of Kyiv’s main bridges. Moscow has also started its attacks on Ukraine’s energy, targeting a thermal power plant and other energy facilities, leaving several neighbourhoods without power and water by morning.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy underlined the apparent shift in Russian tactics in an interview with the Financial Times this week, saying Vladimir Putin had recently ordered his commanders to abandon the rules of war.
“They want Ukrainians to leave the capital … and show that if you don’t have the capital you don’t have the country,” Zelenskyy said in separate comments to reporters.
Until recently, Kyiv had retained a deceptively normal rhythm, while cities closer to the front, including Kharkiv and Dnipro, absorbed the brunt of daily missile and drone attacks. Now, residents joke grimly that the balance is beginning to shift, with those cities at times feeling safer than the capital.
The city is confronting a particularly dangerous combination of an acute shortage of Patriot interceptors for ballistic missiles and a new generation of faster, jet-powered Russian drones that are harder to shoot down.
Kyiv is racing to fast-track a new generation of interceptor drones capable of taking down the jet-powered models. Several are already in use, according to three defence industry sources, though they said it could still take weeks or months to deploy them at a scale sufficient to provide meaningful protection for the capital.
At the same time, Russia’s advances on the battlefield remain relatively slow and are coming at enormous cost.
Moscow captured about 361 sq km in September, according to the military analyst Konrad Muzyka, an increase on recent months but still far short of the pace needed to seize the rest of the Donbas before winter, when offensive operations typically become more difficult.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has clawed back about 126 sq km in a series of counteroffensives in the east, being conducted under the codename Vivaldi. That slower-moving battle on the ground is increasingly at odds with what is happening far behind the front. The contrast reflects a broader shift in the war, as Ukraine’s major cities come under growing pressure.
“You can be quite successful in the land domain, but if you are vulnerable in the air, especially in the rear, that is the vulnerability your opponent is going to exploit,” said Mykola Bielieskov, a military analyst at Ukraine’s government-run National Institute for Strategic Studies.
Ukrainian officials have been warning their European counterparts about the scale of the looming threat. According to the New York Times, Ukraine’s energy minister, Denys Shmyhal, recently briefed European counterparts on an intercepted Russian plan to use as many as 1,000 missiles, drones and bombs against the country’s energy system. The targets included electrical substations, hydroelectric and thermal power plants and boiler houses, in what appeared to be an effort to plunge Ukrainian cities into darkness and cold and create a humanitarian crisis.
“Russia plans to freeze Kyiv out, to throw it back into the stone age,” said one senior western diplomat in Kyiv, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Western diplomats say publicly that they intend to remain in Kyiv, mindful that leaving would hand Moscow a propaganda victory and risk creating the impression that Ukraine was being abandoned. However, privately two senior diplomats said contingency plans were being drawn up to relocate embassies to Lviv or eastern Poland if Russia began deliberately targeting foreign missions.
“The situation is obviously deteriorating fast,” the diplomat said.

articles.title: Russian Ballistic Missiles and Drones Hit Kyiv, Killing One
articles.body:
Russian forces launched a combined ballistic missile-and-drone attack on Kyiv in the early hours of Saturday, Oct. 3, killing one person, injuring two others and sparking fires across several districts of the Ukrainian capital, Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported.
“Explosions in the city. Kyiv is under ballistic attack. Stay in shelters!” Klitschko wrote as the assault unfolded.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He later said Russian forces were continuing to strike the capital with ballistic missiles and warned that the threat of further attacks remained.
Fires were reported in the Sviatoshynskyi and Obolonskyi districts after falling debris struck non-residential areas. Another blaze broke out at a garage cooperative in Sviatoshynskyi district, according to the mayor.
Klitschko later said one man had been killed and two people injured in the attack. One of the wounded was hospitalized, while the second received outpatient treatment.
Air defenses continued operating over the capital against Russian drones after the ballistic strikes, Klitschko said.
In the Holosiivskyi district, falling drone debris ignited grass, though emergency crews later localized the fire.
Targeting capital infrastructure
The early Saturday attack followed several days of intensified Russian strikes on Kyiv and its critical infrastructure.
On Friday, Russian attacks forced authorities to completely close the Southern Bridge and restrict traffic on the Paton and Metro bridges, causing severe congestion across the capital and disrupting travel between the two banks of the Dnipro.
Stubb: Every Russian Threat Should Bring More Support for Ukraine
Russian drones had repeatedly struck the Southern Bridge over the previous two days, damaging the roadway, supports and barriers protecting metro infrastructure.
The latest assault brought ballistic missiles back over the capital in the early hours of Saturday, followed by continuing drone activity and air-defense operations.
The attacks come as Russia intensifies strikes on Ukraine’s transport, energy and other critical infrastructure ahead of winter.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly warned that Moscow is escalating attacks on infrastructure vital to civilian life and has called for stronger air defenses to counter Russia’s expanding missile and drone campaign.
Emergency crews remained deployed across Kyiv Saturday morning, extinguishing fires and assessing damage from the overnight attack.

articles.title: The New York Times obtains a purported Russian plan to cripple Ukraine’s power grid, including by cutting electricity and heat supplies to three major cities by 90%
articles.body:
The New York Times obtains a purported Russian plan to cripple Ukraine’s power grid, including by cutting electricity and heat supplies to three major cities by 90%
Russia plans to disable Ukraine’s entire energy system. Ukrainian authorities have obtained a Russian Defense Ministry document outlining the plan, The New York Times reported. Ukrainian Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal showed it to two European politicians in late September, sources told the newspaper. The Times also obtained a copy of the Russian-language document but said its authenticity could not be verified.
The plan calls for a large-scale campaign using various types of missiles, guided aerial bombs, and drones, including jet-powered models. According to the document, Russia plans to carry out the campaign in three stages:
- First stage: Strikes on substations along Ukraine’s western border to prevent the country from importing electricity from Europe.
- Second stage: Strikes on hydroelectric power plants.
- Third stage: Strikes on substations that supply electricity to the three nuclear power plants still under Ukrainian control. Russian troops occupy Ukraine’s fourth nuclear power plant, the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant.
The campaign’s ultimate goal is to cut off electricity, heat, and water to major Ukrainian cities to provoke a humanitarian crisis.
The plan identifies Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa as the main targets. It calls for reducing electricity and heat supplies to these cities by 90% and disabling a substantial portion of their sewage systems.
The document indicates that Russia plans to eliminate nearly 15 gigawatts of generating capacity — almost as much as Ukraine had at the end of summer 2026, the Times reported.
In August, Shmyhal told Ukraine’s parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, that the country would have 21 gigawatts of generating capacity by the end of the year. That would be enough to meet peak demand, which reached 18 gigawatts last winter. But Russia continues to strike Ukraine’s energy facilities, which could undo the country’s efforts to increase capacity ahead of winter, experts told the Times.
The war in photographs
On October 1, Russian forces deliberately struck a bridge across the Dnipro River in Kyiv for the first time since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Russian drones attacked the bridge three times that day. On the morning of October 2, the Southern Bridge was closed to traffic, and traffic was restricted on the Paton Bridge and the Metro Bridge. Kyiv saw massive traffic jams.
