articles.title: 5 Russian missiles and drones exploded over Moldova's airspace, Sandu says
articles.body:
5 Russian missiles and drones exploded on Moldova's territory in overnight attack against Ukraine, Sandu says
Five Russian air attack weapons, including Banderol missiles and drones, violated Moldova's airspace and exploded on the country's territory during Russia's latest overnight attack against Ukraine, Moldovan President Maia Sandu said on Oct. 3.
"(Russia's) war is dangerously reaching Moldova," Sandu wrote in a post on X, condemning the attack. "Moscow is putting lives at risk across Europe and must be stopped."
Defense Minister Anatolie Nosatyi told journalists that "We have five cases, three missiles and two drones," according to TVR Moldova.
Moldova's Defense Ministry said it tracked several unmanned aircraft on the morning of Oct. 3 near Anenii Noi, Stefan Voda, Tudora, and Causeni. Later, the ministry reported explosions near the villages of Crocmaz, Stefan Voda, Delacau, Puhaceni, Anenii Noi, Bozieni, and Hincesti, as well as in Dubovca, Constantinovca, and Causeni.
No casualties or damage were reported, while police and army teams were dispatched to investigate the incidents.
Russian attacks across Ukraine killed at least eight civilians and injured 83 others over the past day, regional authorities reported on Oct.3.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russia launched 157 Shahed and Gerbera drones, including some jet-powered Shaheds, as well as Parodiya decoy drones.
Russia's attacks on Ukraine frequently lead to violations of Moldova's airspace and explosions on the country's territory.
Drones invaded Moldova's airspace three separate times on Sept. 30, as Russia launched a day-long attack against Ukraine overnight and into the following afternoon.
On Sept. 24, suspected Russian drones crashed in Romania and Moldova overnight, amid a sustained mass drone and missile attack on Ukraine.
On Aug. 16, NATO fighter jets shot down a suspected Russian drone that violated Romanian airspace near the Moldovan border, Romanian Defense Minister Radu Miruta confirmed.
A day later, on Aug. 17, a Russian S-8000 Banderol cruise missile entered Moldovan airspace during a Russian attack on Odesa, before crashing in a cornfield approximately 3 kilometers (1.8 miles) outside of the village of Talmaz, in the Stefan Voda district of Moldova.

articles.title: Russian Strike Hits Liberian Ship in Odesa Port, Killing 1
articles.body:
Russian forces launched a strike against a civilian cargo vessel sailing under the flag of Liberia in an Odesa region port, killing one crew member and injuring three others, the Ukrainian Sea Ports Authority (USPA) reported on Saturday, Oct. 3.
According to an official dispatch published by the USPA, 13 crew members were successfully evacuated to a safe location following the bombardment.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The strike killed a motorman sailor aboard the commercial vessel, while three other crew members sustained varying injuries and were provided emergency medical assistance.
“Russia has once again attacked a civilian vessel,” the port authority stated, noting that emergency crews and port security personnel responded immediately to secure the vessel and assess the destruction.
Targeting of Black Sea commercial vessels
The attack on the Liberian-flagged freighter follows a pattern of Russian strikes directed against foreign commercial shipping operating in and around Odesa’s maritime hubs.
On Sept. 10, a Russian strike hit the foreign-flagged tugboat Tedy – which operated under the flag of Somalia – in the Odesa region, killing two Azerbaijani crew members and wounding eight others.
Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed the fatalities, identifying the deceased as Azerbaijani citizens Aslan Aliyev and Asim Gasimov, while two wounded sailors were hospitalized in the nearby port city of Chornomorsk.
Ukraine’s Ministry of Reconstruction, Infrastructure and Transport condemned that engagement as part of an institutionalized Russian campaign targeting civilian maritime logistics, while Baku cautioned its citizens against transiting active conflict zones.
Russia May Be Using Mesh Relays in Kyiv to Steer Drones, Adviser Says
A similar deadly incident occurred in June, when a Russian strike on a commercial vessel killed five Azerbaijani sailors. Recent months have also seen strikes on commercial ships in Black Sea transit lanes cause the deaths of at least five Indian seafarers, prompting diplomatic demarches from New Delhi to both Moscow and Kyiv.
Kremlin maritime blockade
The strikes reflect Moscow’s declared intention to disrupt maritime transit to Ukrainian ports following the collapse of the UN-brokered Black Sea Grain Initiative.
Responding to international criticism regarding strikes on commercial traffic, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov previously asserted that commercial vessels were being used to transport weapons, ammunition, and fuel for the Armed Forces of Ukraine, declaring that Russian forces would continue destroying such shipping.
Peskov claimed that Russian attacks on transport arteries were retaliatory measures following Ukrainian long-range strikes against Russian economic and refining assets.
Ukrainian authorities and international maritime bodies have categorically rejected the Kremlin’s accusations, emphasizing that the targeted ships are standard merchant vessels engaged in agricultural and bulk cargo transit under international maritime law.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Partners Have Accelerated Repair of Ukrainian F-16s
articles.body:
Ukraine’s industrial partners have accelerated the repair of Ukrainian F-16 fighter jets following intensive use.
This was reported by a spokesperson for the Ukrainian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Heorhiy Tykhyi.
“Our industrial partners providing technical support are not only continuing to deliver the aircraft after major overhauls, but are also doing so increasingly quickly. The turnaround times are getting shorter, not longer,” the spokesperson said.
Problems with maintaining these aircraft stem, in particular, from the fact that some components for early F-16 models are no longer manufactured, and they are becoming increasingly difficult to procure.
“However, recent reports about an allegedly catastrophically low level of aircraft readiness and excessively long maintenance times simply do not correspond to reality,” Tykhyi noted.
Recently, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the Financial Times that about half of the F-16 fighter jets have been in Europe for repairs and maintenance for a long time.
According to him, the return of some aircraft is being delayed to such an extent that Ukraine is losing precious time when the fighter jets are most needed to defend its airspace.
Zelensky noted that Kyiv is seeking assistance from Western partners to shift most of the maintenance work to Ukrainian territory. He said that keeping the aircraft closer to the theater of operations will allow them to be returned to service more quickly.
As of the end of September, Ukrainian pilots flying F-16 fighter jets had already shot down more than 3,150 enemy aerial targets.
Due to a shortage of AIM-120 and AIM-9 air-to-air missiles, Ukrainian F-16 pilots are increasingly firing at drones with 20-mm cannons. To address this, Ukraine is working on a large-scale procurement of 20-mm ammunition for the F-16s.
Last year, to support pre-flight training for F-16 fighter jets, the Come Back Alive Foundation provided the military with mobile maintenance systems.

articles.title: IN BRIEF: Russian gains in Kharkov Region, Dobropolye, Ukrainian losses
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 3. /TASS/. The Russian Defense Ministry reported fighting and territorial gains in the Kharkov Region and Dobropolye, as well as Ukrainian losses and Russian strikes over the past day.
TASS has compiled the ministry’s key statements.
Operations in Kharkov Region
"Enemy formations are being destroyed near Nikolayevka, Nefyodovka, Kupino and Chernoye in the Kharkov Region," the ministry stated.
Battlegroup North troops continue active fighting to liberate Prikolotnoye and Sosnovy Bor.
"Fighting is underway within the encirclement to liberate the settlements of Varvarovka, Lobanovka, and Reznikovo in the Kharkov Region," the Defense Ministry said.
"Ukrainian army losses within the encirclement over the past day included up to 35 personnel and one armored combat vehicle."
Russian troops from the Battlegroup North took control of Novaya Kazachya: "In addition, active offensive operations resulted in establishing control over the settlement of Novaya Kazachya in the Kharkov Region."
Fighting in Dobropolye
"Over the past day, 70 buildings were liberated and more than 20 Ukrainian troops were eliminated," the ministry reported.
"In Dobropolye in the Donetsk People’s Republic, assault groups of the 51st Army, together with marine infantry units, conducted offensive operations in the northwestern, eastern and central parts of the city. Units of the 76th Air Assault Division, advancing west of Dobropolye in the Donetsk People’s Republic, destroyed an enemy position and took control of a section of a forest belt," the ministry said.
Ukrainian troop losses
Ukraine lost approximately 1,325 troops over the past 24 hours as a result of Russian military operations in the special military operation zone.
Ukrainian forces lost more than 250 personnel in the Battlegroup North area of responsibility, over 220 in operations by the Battlegroup West and more than 195 in clashes with the Battlegroup South. They lost up to 385 personnel in clashes with the Battlegroup Center, more than 240 in fighting involving the Battlegroup East and over 35 in clashes with the Battlegroup Dnepr.
Strikes, air defense
"Operational/tactical aircraft, attack unmanned aerial vehicles, missile forces and artillery of Russian battlegroups struck unmanned aerial vehicle storage sites, as well as temporary deployment points of Ukrainian armed formations and foreign mercenaries in 149 areas," the ministry reported.
"Air defenses shot down six guided aerial bombs and 680 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the ministry added.

articles.title: Russian Drones Hit Kyiv’s South Bridge Again as Traffic Collapses
articles.body:
Russian forces struck Kyiv’s South Bridge again on Friday afternoon, according to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko.
The bridge, on which the capital’s green metro line runs, is one of three major crossings across the Dnipro River that separates the city and has come under repeated attack since Thursday.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Klitschko wrote at 5:50 p.m. that the bridge was hit again, and emergency services were heading to the site. Videos circulating on social media also show a dark plume of smoke rising from the bridge against the sunset.
“Another hit on the Southern Bridge. Let me remind you that after several enemy attacks, the bridge is currently closed to traffic and the metro,” Klitschko wrote.
Hours earlier, Klitschko said the metro was awaiting clearance to resume operations across the bridge during yellow-tier air sirens, the lower-risk level of the two-tier system introduced in September.
The attacks prompted authorities to shut down the bridge and restrict traffic on the remaining bridges, leading to gridlocked traffic across the capital on Friday and prompting some locals to walk across the bridges.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said in the wake of the attacks that the Russian President Vladimir Putin had ordered his military commanders to abandon previous constraints on aerial attacks and intensify strikes on civilian sites, with a Russian drone also having slammed into a Ukrainian school during classes on Thursday without exploding.
Ukraine to Speed Up Identification of Fallen Soldiers as Over 26,000 Bodies Returned
Media reports, citing allegedly leaked Russian war plans, also suggest that Moscow is planning to paralyze Ukraine in winter by rendering 90 percent of heating, electricity and water supplies unavailable to Ukrainians as a pressure tactic.

articles.title: US-Russia Peace Talks Eye Multibillion Lukoil Oil Deal
articles.body:
Negotiations between the US administration and Russia aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have expanded to incorporate a multibillion-dollar oil transaction that could benefit Middle Eastern business figures connected to US President Donald Trump’s primary envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
According to The New York Times, the proposed transaction, which requires formal authorization from both the US government and the Kremlin, concerns the extensive international portfolio of Lukoil, Russia’s second-largest oil producer.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The assets under discussion encompass oil extraction concessions in Cameroon and Iraq, major European refining complexes in Bulgaria and Romania, and extensive retail fuel station networks across Europe and the US, including filling stations in New Jersey.
The primary consortium seeking to finalize the acquisition includes American financier Todd Boehly – who contributed $2 million to political entities supporting President Trump – alongside two Middle Eastern investment groups that maintain prior commercial ties with Kushner or the Witkoff family, as well as an entity affiliated with the US government.
The negotiations, which have been underway for several months, were described by eight individuals familiar with the proceedings.
While the reporting noted no indications that Kushner or Witkoff would personally profit from the agreement, the transaction demonstrates the close alignment between private commercial networks and geopolitical statecraft within the administration.
Russia Threatens to Strike Defense Plants in NATO Countries
Regulatory hurdles
Russian President Vladimir Putin raised the prospective sale directly during a confidential Kremlin consultation with Witkoff and Kushner on Sept. 5, according to three individuals briefed on the meeting.
Putin reportedly proposed the transaction as a practical vehicle to demonstrate to the Russian business elite and the domestic public that normal commercial engagement with the US remains achievable.
The American negotiators responded that they would facilitate work on the transaction, viewing the commercial bridge as an instrument to cultivate constructive relations with Moscow while exerting downward pressure on international crude oil benchmarks.
For prospective buyers, US regulatory approval represents a substantial financial upside, as clearing the transaction would lift US sanctions restrictions on the assets and immediately elevate their market capitalization.
Although Lukoil operates formally as a publicly traded private enterprise, decisions governing its strategic divestments are widely treated within Moscow as resting directly with Putin. Consequently, the execution of the multi-continent transaction hinges on political determinations made by Trump and Putin.
The commercial discussions align with Trump’s public statements viewing Russia as a vast economic opportunity, which he has promoted as a framework to incentivize peace.
The initiative has also renewed scrutiny over Trump-affiliated business interests, including the cryptocurrency venture World Liberty Financial, which was co-founded by Witkoff and includes an investor who also maintains an equity stake in the proposed Lukoil buyout consortium.

articles.title: Pete Hegseth just took his personal crusade to a new level | Arwa Mahdawi
articles.body:
Apart from money and McDonald’s, there’s nothing Donald Trump seems to love more than a “big, beautiful” wall. The government is currently spending billions of taxpayer dollars to fulfill the president’s fantasy of lining the US-Mexico border with 30ft steel bollard walls and high-tech surveillance.
What the Trump administration is apparently not so keen on is the wall of separation between church and state. While the president may hawk bibles as a side hustle, he is not exactly devout; he serves only mammon. The top levels of his government, however, are stuffed full of religious fanatics who appear hellbent on remaking the country as a Christian theocracy.
Chief among these is the defense secretary and former Fox News personality Pete Hegseth. When he isn’t screeching about “beardos, weirdos, and wimps”, the man is cosplaying as a megachurch pastor. Hegseth, who has been married three times and paid $50,000 to a woman who accused him of rape in 2017 (he denies the accusation), found God relatively recently. He joined an evangelical church in 2018 and is now busy imposing his own brand of religion on the Pentagon, framing the war on Iran as a modern crusade and instituting monthly prayer services.
Sometimes he blends Pulp Fiction with the Bible at these services; other times he prays for “overwhelming violence of action against those who deserve no mercy”. The Jesus that told people to love their enemies, it seems, is far too woke (and bearded) for Hegseth.
This week, Hegseth took his personal crusade to a whole new level, announcing a new Pentagon Office of Religious Affairs, which reports directly to him. The military he said, was putting on “the full armor of God”. The Pentagon insists that it will not “compel religious participation”, but given Hegseth’s broader efforts to imbue Christianity into the armed forces, it’s hard not to be alarmed. Americans United for Separation of Church and State, which has sued the Pentagon over its worship services, is certainly worried. “All of [Hegseth’s] actions combined with this latest announcement make clear that Hegseth is advancing a Christian Nationalist agenda in the military,” the group said in a statement.
And that agenda seems to go well beyond the military. Hegseth has close ties to Doug Wilson, an extremist pastor and self-described Christian nationalist who thinks that women should not be allowed to vote. In an interview with NPR, Wilson said he doesn’t think his full vision for turning the US into a Christian theocracy will be realized for about 250 years, but he’s taking it step by step. His main focus now is banning abortion and same-sex marriage. While he’s still not a mainstream figure, the likes of Hegseth are pushing him out of the fringes fast. The defense secretary invited Wilson to lead a worship service at the Pentagon in February and has amplified a CNN video where the pastor said women should submit to their husbands.
It’s also not just Hegseth and his extremist pastor that we have to worry about. The Missouri senator Josh Hawley proudly said in a 2024 speech that he is “advocating Christian nationalism” and has been pushing to overturn access to abortion medication in the name of these beliefs. The House speaker Mike Johnson is connected to strongly Christian nationalist views. Meanwhile, JD Vance recently appeared on an evangelical podcast where he said is doing as much of “God’s work as possible” and is OK “if that leads to the end times”, which are apparently “coming”.
I’m an atheist, but the way things are going, the end times are beginning to sound appealing. Let’s just pray it starts with the end of this administration.
The underground world of US abortion pill mules
Nineteen states and Washington DC have codified shield laws that protect health providers who prescribe and mail the abortion medications mifepristone and misoprostol to people in states with abortion bans. But these protections are under attack: in the latest attempt to curtail access to the medication, three attorneys general in anti-abortion states (Louisiana, Alabama, Arkansas) filed a lawsuit with the US supreme court challenging these laws. It’s not surprising then that some activists are bypassing the legal and medical systems and taking matters into their own hands: using volunteers to obtain abortion pills abroad and then distribute them to community support networks across the US. “It really doesn’t matter what [state and federal authorities] do legally – we will continue,” one activist told Mother Jones. They added: “There may come a time where we are one of the only, if not the only, option for the nation.”
Margot Robbie is changing her legal name after a decade of marriage
“We don’t know why she has done this, but it has nonetheless caused a stir,” writes the always hilarious Rebecca Shaw in the Guardian about Margot Robbie becoming Margot Ackerley. “We got the usual discourse of blah blah tradition, blah blah patriarchy, blah blah women’s individual choice and so on.” Instead of engaging in this discourse, Shaw has a very practical solution for how married couples should choose a surname.
Laws on intoxication and consent scrutinized after Cornell rape allegations
New York is one of 19 states that has “voluntary intoxication” laws, which some people argue effectively serve as a legal loophole protecting sexual offenders. If you as a victim were voluntarily under the influence of drugs or alcohol, you cannot claim that you were mentally incapacitated during an assault unless you can show that you were unconscious or otherwise physically helpless. After the Cornell gang-rape allegations became national news, this law is now facing increasing scrutiny. The prosecutor Matthew Van Houten has said that that the fact the Jane Doe in the case voluntarily took drugs is partly why criminal charges were never brought. Kathy Hochul, New York’s governor, has criticized this aspect of the law and appointed the state attorney general Letitia James to oversee the case after she “lost faith” in Van Houten.
The horror of the Cornell rape case is how ordinary it is
“Sexual assault … reveals that law is applied selectively, according to the needs of power,” writes Moria Donegan. “Every court and every university, and every institution will say: ‘We take sexual violence extremely seriously.’ And every one will find, with uncanny consistency, reasons not to take it very seriously at all.”
Take a look at the latest Google Maps satellite images of Gaza
… and then tell me this isn’t a genocide. While it isn’t a mainstay of the news, South Lebanon is also systematically being wiped off the map by Israel.
Influencer Alix Earle says she’s never read a book
“Like, maybe Dr Seuss,” she added in a chat with Interview Mag. I had never actually heard of Earle before seeing this headline, but I have certainly heard about the US literacy crisis. No doubt Earle is exaggerating for attention, but this sort of proud anti-intellectualism is so depressing. No wonder Trump is the president.
The US is spelled wrong in a White House accord on ‘super intelligence’
The president and some top tech titans signed a voluntary accord on “super intelligence” this week to allay fears about AI. Alas, they managed to misspell the United States as “Unites States”. Is the “super intelligence” in the room with us now? Forget AI, it’s Trump’s intelligence I’m worried about.
- Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

articles.title: Russia rehearses invasion and occupation of Central Asian country during military exercises – videos
articles.body:
Russia rehearses invasion and occupation of Central Asian country during military exercises – videos
Russian forces have practised seizing territory and "creating a security zone" in a neighbouring Central Asian country during the Centre-2026 military exercises in Chelyabinsk Oblast.
Source: Russian propaganda media outlets; the Kremlin press service
Details: The exercises are taking place from 28 September to 3 October. They involve 47,000 military personnel, 2,000 pieces of military equipment, 90 aircraft and 77 warships and other vessels. Military contingents from Belarus, China, Kyrgyzstan, Mongolia, Pakistan and Tajikistan are taking part in the exercises.
Russian ruler Vladimir Putin arrived at the Chebarkul training ground accompanied by a military helicopter. Several sections of roads in the area were closed to traffic for three days because of his visit, completely isolating the city of Chebarkul.
According to the official scenario announced by Russia's Defence Ministry, the exercises are designed to practise repelling aggression on the Central Asian front and ensuring security in the Caspian region.
Meanwhile, Deputy Defence Minister Yunus-bek Yevkurov, reporting to Russian ruler Vladimir Putin on the progress of the exercises, said that the troops were practising not only repelling an attack but also "creating a security zone in adjacent territories".
"The coalition force is repelling the main attack on the South Urals front, has restored its positions and, since 2 October, has been conducting offensive operations to liberate the captured territory and create a security zone in the adjacent territory," he said.
The Kremlin noted that the exercises involved units that are not taking part in the war against Ukraine. However, Putin stressed that all tasks were being conducted taking into account the experience of warfare in Ukraine.
Of the countries that could fit the description of the "aggressor country" in the scenario, Kazakhstan is the most plausible, as it has access to the Caspian Sea and borders Russia's Chelyabinsk Oblast. During the exercises, four long-range aircraft carried out strikes on critical facilities belonging to the simulated enemy.
Background:
- Russia has previously held similar large-scale military exercises. In particular, around 128,000 military personnel officially took part in the Centre-2019 exercises, while around 95,000 people participated in the Centre-2015 exercises.
- During the 2019 exercises, Russian troops practised neutralising a simulated state in southwestern Russia that had allegedly started a war and was spreading terrorism.

Kyiv • UNN

articles.title: DPRK conducts exercise involving launch of intermediate-range strategic missiles — KCNA
articles.body:
PYONGYANG, October 3. /TASS/. The DPRK has conducted an exercise involving the launch of intermediate-range strategic missiles, Kim Yo Jong, a department director of the Central Committee of the Workers' Party of Korea, said, according to the KCNA news agency.
"At dawn today, an exercise involving the launch of intermediate-range strategic missiles toward the east coast of our country was carried out," the statement said.
According to Kim Yo Jong, officials from the General Missile Bureau reported to the head of state, who personally observed the exercise, that new technologies enable the missiles to follow at least four different flight trajectories depending on the target and mission. She also reiterated Pyongyang’s previously stated claims about the missiles’ ability to alter their trajectories at low altitudes and their use of artificial intelligence technologies.
"In other words, this effectively means that it is impossible to evade such a strike," Kim Yo Jong said. She added that when a wave-like trajectory was employed, enemy detection systems lost track of the target after the initial ascent phase.
The DPRK official also addressed assessments of the missiles’ flight range. She noted that South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff reported a range of more than 700 kilometers, while Japan’s Ministry of Defense estimated it at approximately 680 kilometers. Pyongyang views the discrepancy as evidence of the missiles’ distinctive flight characteristics and the limitations of existing surveillance systems.
Kim Yo Jong said the DPRK had observed a similar scenario four times, adding that this, in Pyongyang’s view, confirms the effectiveness of the special flight mode employed by the missiles.

Russia strikes key Kiev bridge (VIDEOS)
The Russian military has struck Kiev’s Northern Bridge over the Dnieper River to undermine Ukraine’s military logistics, the Defense Ministry said.
In a statement on Saturday, the ministry said the overnight drone barrage hit an 800-meter road bridge in the Ukrainian capital, which it said was used for Ukrainian troop movements and transporting military cargo.
Officials also said drones struck the Gostomel logistics center in Kiev Region where military supplies are stored. Another attack hit a dry-cargo vessel carrying dual-use equipment as it sailed through the northwestern Black Sea toward Odessa, the statement added.
Kiev Mayor Vitaly Klitschko confirmed that the Northern Bridge was hit, adding that the road surface and trolleybus contact network were damaged and that traffic was suspended. Videos shared by Ukrainian media show major traffic jams in one of the capital’s districts.
There are eight major road and rail bridges connecting the eastern and western parts of Kiev. Earlier this week, Russia targeted the Pivdennyi (southern) Bridge, saying it was “facilitating troop movements and the logistical delivery of military cargo for the Ukrainian military units in Donbass.”
A local official told Strana.ua that the bridge carries up to 90% of transit road traffic between Ukraine’s left- and right-bank regions and also handles a significant share of military shipments.
Following the strikes, Ukrainian MP Vladimir Kreidenko said lawmakers are considering ferries and temporary pontoon crossings if serious damage to the bridges leads to prolonged traffic disruptions.
Russia has intensified strikes on military-related logistics and defense industrial base in recent weeks in response to Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky’s 40-day PR ‘pressure campaign’, which included long-range strikes targeting oil refineries and civilian infrastructure deep inside Russia.

articles.title: Ukraine lost another MiG-29 and its pilot on Thursday. It needs the jets to guard its cities, and almost none are left to replace them
articles.body:
- Ukraine has lost another Mikoyan MiG-29 fighter as well as its pilot
- The Ukrainian MiG fleet is slowly dwindling owing to combat losses and wear and tear
- The Ukrainian air force is acquiring new Western types to replace the MiGs and other ex-Soviet jets
Ukraine has lost another Mikoyan MiG-29 fighter and its pilot. The Thursday shoot-down extends the steady attrition of the Ukrainian air force MiG fleet, potentially drawing down the fleet to its pre-war strength.
That means Ukraine may have lost as many of the twin-engine, supersonic MiG-29s as it has received from its allies or restored from surplus stocks since February 2022.
It's an ominous milestone. The Soviet-vintage MiG-29 is no longer the Ukrainian air force's most important fighter. That honorific belongs to the air force's ex-European Lockheed Martin F-16s.
But the MiG-29 is still the air force's second most important fighter—and will remain so through 2027 as Ukraine awaits its first ex-Swedish Saab Gripens, due early next year, and French-made Dassault Rafales, due from 2028. Ukraine sorties MiG-29s for ground attack missions targeting Russian troop concentrations, strikes on Russian air defense systems, and air defense sorties over Ukrainian cities and ports.
The air force announced the loss of the MiG-29 and its pilot, Capt. Marat Mambetov, shortly after it occurred on Thursday. Mambetov, 25, was a flight commander in the 40th Tactical Aviation Brigade, known as the "Ghost of Kyiv" brigade. "Flying a MiG-29 fighter jet, [Mambetov] carried out missile and bomb strikes against Russian occupiers along one of the front-line directions," the air force stated. "During the mission, his aircraft was hit by an enemy missile. The pilot ejected, but tragically did not survive."
It's the 37th confirmed combat loss of a Ukrainian MiG-29 since Russia widened its war on Ukraine in February 2022, according to a tally by the Oryx open-source intelligence collective. Oryx has also registered damage to an additional three Ukrainian MiG-29s.
Thirty-seven write-offs, plus the likely grounding of several previously flyable MiG-29s owing to intensive wear and tear since 2022, may have reduced the Ukrainian air force's MiG-29 fleet to around three dozen active jets.
Fighter subtraction
The math is simple. The air force probably had between 30 and 35 MiG-29s in service when Russia attacked in February 2022. As losses cut into the fleet, Poland donated 14 surplus MiGs, Slovakia donated 10, and Azerbaijan reportedly donated three. Meanwhile, Ukrainian engineers tapped a global pipeline of spare parts to reactivate an estimated 20 grounded MiG-29s moldering in hangars at various Ukrainian airfields.
That's as many as 82 MiGs in and, as of Thursday, 37 out owing to Russian action—plus additional jets grounded due to airframe fatigue. The resulting active fleet should number around three dozen planes, around as many as Ukraine had on the eve of the wider war.
There aren't many more old MiGs that Ukraine could obtain to bolster the fleet. Poland still has as many as nine very tired airframes, but Kyiv and Warsaw have consistently failed to negotiate a transfer. There may yet be a few ex-Soviet MiG-29s, grounded for years or even decades, that Ukrainian engineers can restore to flightworthy status. Other than that, options are scarce.
Ukraine’s Swedish radar planes have flown inside Russian missile range for six months. None has been shot down.
The three dozen MiGs still in the inventory may have to last a little while alongside the few survivors of Ukraine's other Soviet-vintage warplanes, including Sukhoi Su-27s, Sukhoi Su-24s, and Sukhoi Su-25s.
Older Western types—the 80 or so F-16s European allies have pledged, about half delivered, as well as potentially a dozen or so ex-French Dassault Mirage 2000s—are steadily replacing the ex-Soviet jets. (So far, Ukraine has lost five F-16s and one Mirage.) Next year, the transformation of the Ukrainian air force from a largely Soviet-equipped force to a largely Western-equipped force will accelerate when the first of 32 Gripens arrive. Sixteen Rafales are to follow from 2028.
Barring catastrophic combat losses among Western types and assuming Ukraine can maintain and arm these new warplanes, by the end of 2027, the air force may not need its remaining MiGs and Sukhois, which by then could be very tired.
Russian missiles are steadily reducing the MiG and Sukhoi fleets, effectively forcing Ukraine to switch to new types.

As he left the White House for a campaign rally in Alabama on Friday, Donald Trump was asked by a reporter if he had “jumped the gun” by announcing on Wednesday that South Korea had agreed to pay for a $54bn natural gas pipeline in Alaska, only for a Korean official to contradict him on Thursday, saying that Korea had only agreed to “initiate a review” of the possible investment.
“No, I didn’t jump the gun,” Trump replied. “Let’s see if they don’t want to do it. That’s okay with me. I’ll just charge them more.”
When he announced the pipeline project in an Oval Office ceremony on Wednesday, the president claimed that the Korean investment was part of a deal he struck in 2025, to lower tariffs on imports from South Korea in return for billions of dollars of investments in the US.
“They said they didn’t sign it?” Trump asked the reporter on Friday. “Tell them if they don’t sign shortly, I’m going to double it up, okay?”
As he apparently threatened to double tariffs on imports from South Korea, Trump repeated his incorrect claim that tariffs on imports are fees paid by the country that exports goods to the US. In fact, tariffs are, as the US supreme court clarified when it ruled many of Trump’s tariffs an illegal form of taxation on Americans, paid by US importers.
This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments:
Confronted with the fact that South Korean officials say they did not agree to invest $54bn to build a natural gas pipeline in Alaska, as Donald Trump announced they had on Wednesday, the president threatened to double tariffs on South Korean goods imported to the US unless they agree to make the investment.
Ignoring public sentiment, that his war with Iran and failure to tackle inflation has hurt the country, Trump told supporters in Alabama that his second term is “the most successful presidency in history.”

A federal judge blocked the Trump administration from constructing a border wall at Big Bend national park in Texas until a lawsuit opposing it is resolved.

Senator Adam Schiff reaffirmed his support on Friday for legislation introduced this week by Democrats that would stop the Trump administration from closing archives of government records in California and Illinois.
“The administration is threatening access to historical and irreplaceable records, including closing down one facility in California that is home to countless photos and family heirlooms,” Schiff said in a statement. “Congress must exercise its oversight power to save decades of regional and national history.”
Schiff and his California colleague Alex Padilla joined two Illinois Democrats, Tammy Duckworth and Dick Durbin, to introduce the National Archives Protection Act, which would ensure archival records remain accessible to the public.
One of the facilities the administration reportedly plans to close, in the San Francisco Bay area, hosts original records from the US supreme court case United States v. Wong Kim Ark, which affirmed that the constitution grants birthright citizenship to anyone born in the US.
Trump concludes remarks to supporters in Alabama claiming 'the most successful presidency in history'
The blessed sound of YMCA has just been heard in Mobile, Alabama, signaling that Donald Trump’s rally speech is over.
In his remarks, which included a plea to supporters to “just close your eyes and pretend I’m on the ballot,” Trump mentioned various Republican candidates in passing, but mainly made the case for himself, casting his second term in office as an unalloyed triumph, marred only by “bad press”.
“If you want to keep America the strongest, most successful nation the world has ever seen – we are right now more respected than at any time in the history of our country, and that’s where the bad press,” Trump said, “you have to vote Republican.”
“Just think of what the Trump administration and our Republican majorities have accomplished in less than two years’ time,” he went on. “Nobody’s ever seen this before. Nobody’s ever done it. We have the most successful- it’s not two years; it’s substantially less - the most successful presidency in history.”

“A great Republican strategist, a great person, a killer,” Trump said. “When she’s angry at you, it’s a very terrible situation. Laura Loomer. Thank you. Laura. She’s great.”
Loomer, an influential outside Trump adviser whose extreme views and statements led to criticism of Trump during the 2024 campaign, when she traveled with him to events, posted a photograph of herself with Trump on Air Force One earlier in the day.
Trump regales supporters in Alabama with familiar tales, some imaginary
Donald Trump is regaling supporters in Alabama with a version of his rally speech that includes many of his familiar boasts and grievances, a number of which are based on entirely imaginary claims.
To take one example, Trump once again claimed that he was instantly blamed for high prices by the media after just one day in office.
“I took over and in my first news conference on January 21st … a day after that beautiful day we had in quite cold weather, the inauguration. A day later, I had a news conference and they said, ‘affordability’. I said, ‘I just got here. What do they mean?’” Trump insisted, despite the fact that he was, in fact, asked no questions about affordability at all during that news conference.
In the first weeks of his administration, Trump repeatedly claimed that prices were dropping and then, at a cabinet meeting two months into his second term, claimed for the first time that he had been unfairly blamed for high egg prices. “When I came in, after one week, they were screaming at me about eggs. Eggs had nothing to do with me,” the president said on 24 March 2025. He has repeated the false claim that reporters blamed him for high food prices dozens of times since.
Later in the address, Trump said, as he has dozens of times since he visited Saudi Arabia in May 2025, that the Saudi king had praised him for almost instantly turning around the US economy.
“Less than two years ago, our country was dead,” Trump told supporters in Alabama on Friday night. “Remember that? I told you, the king of Saudi Arabia was talking to me. In August, crews contracted by US Customs and border protection (CBP) began bulldozing at the mouth of Big Bend National Park’s famed Santa Elena Canyon. The plan was to construct new border security infrastructure, which was dubbed the “smart wall”.

She noted that “wages are up over last year” – despite the fact they have not kept up with inflation.

articles.title: Poroshenko calls on EU to speed up conversion of defense funding into military contracts
articles.body:
Ukrainian MP and leader of the European Solidarity party Petro Poroshenko, during a meeting in Brussels with EU Commissioner for Defence and Space Andrius Kubilius, discussed deepening defense cooperation between Ukraine and the European Union and called for faster financing and implementation of joint defense projects.
"Russia's tactic of massive use of jet-powered drones requires a rapid search for effective and cost-efficient means of interception and countermeasures, including modern detection systems, electronic warfare capabilities and counter-drone solutions. Particular attention was paid to new technologies, joint Ukrainian-European developments and their rapid scaling, including through the full use of the potential of the Ukraine-EU Drone Alliance," Poroshenko wrote on Facebook following the meeting.
According to him, the parties also discussed EU financing for Ukraine's defense sector and the timely coverage of expenditures on the procurement of drones, missiles, ammunition and air defense systems.
"My main message to our partners is that European funding must be converted into military contracts as quickly as possible, contracts into production - preferably joint production - and production into real capabilities on the battlefield," Poroshenko emphasized.
Separately, he called for the swift integration of Ukraine's defense-industrial complex into the European defense architecture, noting that this is in the interests of both Ukraine and the security of the European continent.

articles.title: Zelenskyy expects 400 jet-powered drone interceptors to be produced in October, but their effectiveness varies
articles.body:
Zelenskyy expects 400 jet-powered drone interceptors to be produced in October, but their effectiveness varies
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukraine could produce around 400 units of one model of high-speed interceptor drone for countering Russian jet-powered drones as early as October, but there are questions over their effectiveness.
Source: Zelenskyy in an interview with the Financial Times, as cited by the president's press service
Details: Zelenskyy said F-16 fighter jets currently destroy 50-60% of jet-powered drones. This is one method, and Ukraine is working extensively to obtain weapons for the F-16s. The second method is high-speed interceptors. Ukraine is currently testing five interceptor models.
However, their effectiveness is problematic: it is 70% one day and 30% the next. Therefore, the answer to the question "When can we scale up the production?" is that Ukraine does not have billions to produce a million ineffective interceptors.
The main issue is the engines. Zelenskyy said Ukraine imports a lot and produces some itself, but these volumes are insufficient.
Quote: "So out of these five samples, some were used five times, some ten, and some only once. But you had one, and destroyed one Russian drone. This is the problem. I don't know the exact date, but in October, we will have 400 of these interceptors. And it is normal when you use 400 interceptors over several days of attacks, and you say, 'Look, guys, sorry, but it destroys only 10%. It doesn't work.' Or, for example, if it is 30% or more, 'Great, guys, you have to work a little bit on it, and when the percentage is 60-70% – huge success'."

articles.title: U.S. in mega deal to build more long-range anti-air missiles
articles.body:
The U.S. Navy has awarded Raytheon a five-year contract worth up to $24.4 billion to accelerate production of the Standard Missile-6, its principal long-range anti-air and anti-surface weapon.
Announced on 1 October by Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao, the multi-year procurement agreement includes two additional option years. The U.S. Navy says the long-term commitment is intended to give the RTX business the stability and predictability needed to expand production capacity, while delivering cost savings through a negotiated deal rather than year-by-year buys.
“Maritime strength demands weapons at speed and scale,” Cao said in the release. “This investment expands production and delivers the firepower our warfighters need to fight, win, and come home safe.”
The SM-6 has become one of the most versatile weapons in the surface fleet’s inventory. Fired from the Mk 41 Vertical Launch System aboard Arleigh Burke-class destroyers and Ticonderoga-class cruisers, it can engage aircraft, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles in their terminal phase, and can also be used against surface ships. Its active radar seeker allows it to engage targets beyond the horizon of the launching ship when cued by other sensors, a key element of the U.S. Navy’s Cooperative Engagement Capability. U.S. warships have fired SM-6s in combat during operations in the Red Sea and Middle East since late 2023, including against Houthi anti-ship missiles, drawing down stocks of a weapon that costs several million dollars per round.
Adm. Daryl Caudle, Chief of Naval Operations, linked the contract directly to the size of the fleet’s magazines. “Combat credibility depends on having enough weapons, produced at the speed and scale the Fleet requires,” he said. “This SM-6 award gives industry the demand signal and stability to expand production, strengthen the munitions industrial base, and build the magazine depth our Fleet needs. That is the Foundry delivering for the Fleet – and ensuring our Sailors have the combat power to fight and win.”
The award is being managed by the U.S. Navy’s Portfolio Acquisition Executive (PAE) Munitions, an organisation responsible for the development, procurement and delivery of naval munitions and strike capabilities. It follows a recent Tomahawk contract, which the service describes as part of the same effort to speed up weapons production across the portfolio.
“This award demonstrates what is possible when the Department leverages innovative acquisition approaches to deliver capability at the speed of relevance,” said Van Hendrey, Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Munitions. “Through PAE Munitions, we are bringing together the authorities, resources, and partnerships needed to accelerate production, reduce costs, and strengthen the industrial base that supports our warfighters.”
Raytheon produces the SM-6 at its facilities in Tucson, Arizona, with final assembly at Redstone Arsenal in Huntsville, Alabama. The missile has also been cleared for export to a number of U.S. allies, with Japan and Australia among the nations to have pursued it for their own air defence destroyers.
According to the U.S. Navy, the agreement will support a larger workforce, higher manufacturing throughput and stronger supply chains for the missile, as part of a wider push to rebuild the defence industrial base and keep Navy and Marine Corps forces supplied with advanced weapons.

articles.title: Russia attacked Ukraine with 157 drones - how many destroyed and what is known about the strikes

Russia attacked Ukraine with 157 drones - how many destroyed and what is known about the strikes
Kyiv • UNN
Overnight, Russia launched 157 drones at Ukraine; air defense forces destroyed or suppressed 131 of them. Strikes were recorded at 12 locations.
Russia struck Ukraine with 157 drones during the night of October 3. Of these, 131 were shot down or suppressed. UNN reports this, citing data from the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
What Russia used to strike and where the attack came from
According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, during the night of October 3 (from 18:00 on October 2), the enemy attacked with 157 Shahed-type attack UAVs (45 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and Parodiya-type decoy drones from the following directions: Bryansk, Primorsko-Akhtarsk — Russia, the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk, and the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea — Hvardiiske.

The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to preliminary data, as of 09:00, air defense forces had shot down/suppressed 131 enemy Shahed-type UAVs, Gerbera drones, and drones of other types

Hits by the enemy’s air attack assets were recorded at 12 locations, while downed targets (debris) fell at 5 locations.

articles.title: Trump can win against Iran only in his imagination: Rezaei
articles.body:
Major General Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council (SNSC), made the remarks in a post on X on Friday, where wrote, “After one failure after another, the worst president in American history just keeps talking—and talking—and now his words have even outrun his own fantasies.”

articles.title: Russia turns helicopter missile into truck-mounted weapon
articles.body:
- Russia fired its new truck-mounted Izdeliye 347 launcher with a modified LMUR missile at mock artillery positions during the Tsentr-2026 exercise.
- The Defense Ministry says the system can hit stationary and moving targets up to 20 km away, with operator guidance in the final phase.
Russia has fired a guided missile from its attack helicopters off a truck, using a new ground launcher called Izdeliye 347, or “Product 347,” against mock artillery positions during its Tsentr-2026 exercise.
The Russian Defense Ministry said on Oct. 2 that the system carries a modified version of the LMUR light multipurpose guided missile and can hit stationary and moving targets up to 20 km (12 miles) away. During the main stage of the drills at the Chebarkul training range in the Chelyabinsk region, crews used it to strike artillery positions that had been found by aerial reconnaissance.
The ministry said the launcher is mounted on a truck and that an operator can steer the missile onto the target in the final part of its flight. It did not say how many missiles each launcher carries, what chassis it uses, who builds it, or when it could enter service.
The LMUR, also known as Izdeliye 305 and the Kh-39, is built by the KBM design bureau in Kolomna, part of Rostec’s High Precision Systems holding. It weighs about 105 kg (231 pounds) and carries a 25 kg (55-pound) high-explosive fragmentation warhead. The basic version has a stated range of 14.5 km, and a longer-range variant reportedly reaches beyond 25 km.
Russia fields the missile on its Mi-28NM and Ka-52M attack helicopters and has used it widely against Ukrainian forces. Its main advantage is that it does not need to see the target at launch. The missile flies toward given coordinates using satellite navigation, then sends video from its thermal seeker back to the operator, who picks out the target and guides it in. That lets helicopter crews fire from well behind the front, out of range of most Ukrainian short-range air defenses.
A ground version would give Russian units the same kind of long-range, man-in-the-loop strike capability without risking a helicopter. The concept is similar to Israel’s Spike NLOS, which is fired from helicopters, vehicles and ships.
Russia has tried this before. Several years ago, the Defense Ministry worked on a project codenamed Baikal to adapt the LMUR for ground launch. That design used an armored tracked vehicle, similar in concept to the Khrizantema-S anti-tank system, and was also meant to engage slow, low-flying aerial targets. Its fate was never made public.
Izdeliye 347 takes a different approach, putting the missile on an unarmored truck instead of a tracked combat vehicle.
The launcher was one of several new or rarely seen systems Russia showed at Tsentr-2026, which ran from Sept. 28 to Oct. 3 and involved more than 47,000 troops, according to the Defense Ministry.

articles.title: North Korea launches ballistic missile after Seoul demands apology over wounded soldiers
articles.body:
North Korea fired a ballistic missile towards the sea on Saturday, South Korea and Japan said, a day after it rejected Seoul’s accusation of its mines wounding soldiers.
The missile was launched from the Wonsan area at about 6.30am towards the East Sea – also known as the Sea of Japan – and flew more than 700km (434 miles), the South Korean military said. Seoul and Washington were analysing the test for details, it added.
Japan’s coast guard, citing the defence ministry, said the object may have been a ballistic missile and appeared to have come down, warning ships to take precautions.
South Korea’s military said it heightened its monitoring of any further missile tests and would share intelligence with the US and Japan. The South Korean presidential office’s national security council convened an emergency meeting on Saturday to assess the situation.
Pyongyang’s Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of ruler Kim Jong-un, issued a statement on Friday that dismissed Seoul’s demand for an apology for what it said were North Korean mines that seriously wounded South Korean soldiers in the demilitarised zone – the heavily guarded buffer between the two Koreas.
South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, had urged Pyongyang on Thursday to return to dialogue, despite his military demanding an apology a day earlier. Kim Yo-jong responded by calling Seoul “really despicable” and ridiculing Lee’s latest overture, calling it “the climax of the farce that everyone should watch”.
Kim also warned that Pyongyang was “ready for anything” Seoul might do over the mine blast – remarks followed the next morning by North Korea’s ballistic missile launch.
South Korea said this week that North Korean mines caused the blast that injured three South Korean soldiers on a reconnaissance mission inside the 4km-wide buffer zone that stretches across the Korean peninsula.
The missile test might be an attempt by Pyongyang to draw a response from South Korea to the sister’s statement, said Cheong Seong-chang, vice-president at the Sejong Institute in Seoul, a research centre on North Korean affairs. North Korea might also have tested a new type of missile, he added.
North Korea has launched missile tests on more than 10 occasions so far this year. Some came after North Korea protested against joint military drills between Seoul and Washington.
North Korea has ramped up hostility against the South in recent years, disavowing unification as a national goal and calling South Korea its “primary foe”.
With Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Russia Orders Surge in European Hybrid Attacks
articles.body:
Russia has ordered its intelligence services to “step up” hybrid operations across EU and NATO countries, including possible sabotage targeting military facilities, critical infrastructure and communications systems, Ukraine’s military intelligence agency has warned.
The Military Intelligence of Ukraine (HUR) said Moscow planned to use agents recruited across Europe by Russia’s GRU military intelligence service and FSB security service to carry out the operations.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The intelligence services of aggressor state Russia have been instructed to step up their activities in EU and NATO countries,” HUR said in a statement on Friday.
It said the operations were aimed at undermining support for Ukraine and weakening NATO’s capabilities.
“Military facilities, critical infrastructure and communications systems are among the targets being monitored by Russian intelligence services,” the agency said.
“Potential targets include Starlink satellite internet receiving stations located in European countries,” it added.
HUR said it had warned Ukraine’s international partners about Russia’s plans.
Starlink facility targeted in Poland
The warning comes just over a week after a fire at a Starlink satellite communications ground station in Wola Krobowska, a village in central Poland, which Polish authorities are investigating as suspected Russian-linked sabotage.

Prosecutors say the fire was deliberately set, allegedly to disrupt Starlink internet traffic and communications in Poland and other countries in Central and Eastern Europe. No one has yet been charged in the investigation.
Starlink, a satellite internet system operated by billionaire Elon Musk’s US aerospace company SpaceX, has become a key part of Ukraine’s war effort, providing internet connectivity for frontline communications, drone operations and battlefield command.
Sabotage fears grow
The EU, the majority of whose member states also belong to the Western military alliance NATO, has been on heightened alert for acts of sabotage and other hybrid attacks since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of neighboring Ukraine in 2022.
Concerns have grown amid a recent uptick in such incidents. Last month, Berlin said Russia was behind a foiled drone attack targeting Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle Airport in eastern Germany, a key logistics hub for NATO and Kyiv.
Moscow has repeatedly denied involvement in hybrid operations against European countries.

articles.title: Russian linked to GRU may have organized sabotage at Leipzig Airport — media
articles.body:
Russian linked to GRU may have organized sabotage at Leipzig Airport — media
The Telegraph and Welt am Sonntag reported this in a joint investigation, according to Ukrinform.
According to classified intelligence documents from Germany, Lithuania and Poland, as well as interviews with senior Western intelligence officials, Levushkin arrived in Germany via Turkey this summer to prepare an attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport, one of the key military-logistics hubs through which support for Ukraine is provided. According to the media reports, he allegedly acted together with Belarusian intermediary agent Andrei Karshakov.
The reports note that Levushkin, who presents an ordinary lifestyle on social media and is interested in motorcycle racing, operated in Germany as a GRU "disposable agent."
Journalists report that, according to German intelligence, Levushkin conducted reconnaissance near the airport on July 31. A week before the attack, he rented a car at Berlin Airport and drove it to several locations where investigators believe materials intended for the sabotage may have been stored.
Five days later, a drone carrying approximately 1.8 kilograms of Semtex explosives crashed into the wing of a parked Ukrainian An-124 cargo aircraft. After the collision, the drone fell onto the runway, but no explosion occurred. German investigators believe Levushkin planned the operation and entrusted its direct execution to Karshakov. According to intelligence information, the explosives may have been brought into Germany through Bulgaria and Serbia, concealed in compartments of trucks, the media reported.
Investigators also identified similarities between the Leipzig attack and other Russian sabotage operations involving drones and explosives against targets in Poland, Lithuania and Germany.
According to the media reports, Levushkin maintained contacts for many years with Denis Smolyaninov, who is considered one of the organizers of Russian sabotage operations in Europe. Britain imposed sanctions on him last year.
According to the publication, a Lithuanian intelligence report from December 2025 stated that Smolyaninov headed the Ukrainian direction within the GRU, specialized in psychological operations and was linked to covert sabotage campaigns in Europe.
According to German intelligence, the Leipzig attack is linked to GRU Unit 29155, which intelligence officials say plays a key role in Russia's sabotage operations in Europe.
German security authorities reportedly believe that Moscow seeks to make Europeans perceive support for Ukraine as risky in order to influence public debate and weaken support for Kyiv.
A senior German intelligence official said that incidents that had previously occurred only in isolated cases were now being observed on a much larger scale, adding that Germany was increasingly becoming a theater of military operations for Russian intelligence services.
As Ukrinform reported, a drone carrying an explosive device was discovered near a Ukrainian An-124 transport aircraft at Leipzig/Halle Airport. It was subsequently neutralized by federal police specialists.
At the time, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt described the incident as a "hybrid attack scenario," while emphasizing that the possible organizer had not yet been identified.
German media later reported that the An-124 aircraft was loaded with ammunition.

articles.title: UK sanctions seven Russians over deportation of Ukrainian children
articles.body:
UK sanctions seven Russians over deportation of Ukrainian children
The United Kingdom has imposed sanctions on seven people involved in Russia's programme of forced deportation and "re-education" of Ukrainian children.
Source: Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia (Life)
Details: The list includes the chairman of the board of Russia's Movement of the First, heads of its branches in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, and the chair of the board of trustees of Russia's National Centre for Assistance to Missing and Affected Children.
Bring Kids Back UA, a Ukrainian government-led effort to bring Ukrainian children home from temporarily Russian-occupied territories, told Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia about the people included on the sanctions list.
Who has been sanctioned?
The list includes Artur Orlov, chairman of the board of the Movement of the First, a Russian state-backed social movement for children and young people. Orlov is a Russian officer, tank battalion commander and combatant in the war against Ukraine. Russian ruler Vladimir Putin appointed him to head the movement in 2024.
Five heads of the movement's regional branches in the temporarily occupied territories of Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia oblasts and Crimea have also been sanctioned:
- Denis Chernobai
- Riyal Aliyev
- Aleksei Lavrentyev
- Viktoria Kostromina
- Yekaterina Kozyr.
Russia established the Movement of the First in 2022 on Putin's initiative as one of the tools for militarising children. According to a report by the OSCE Moscow Mechanism expert mission, it has more than 344,000 members in the occupied territories alone.
The list also includes Yelena Milskaya, chair of the board of trustees of Russia's National Centre for Assistance to Missing and Affected Children.
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine has information that in October 2022 she used the centre's volunteers as cover for the mass abduction and illegal deportation of Ukrainian children, including orphans, from the occupied territories of Ukraine to Krasnodar Krai via Crimea.
At least three of the seven people – Orlov, Chernobai and Milskaya – have been sanctioned by Canada, while Milskaya has also been sanctioned by the EU.
"The Movement of the First in the occupied territories is not about children's clubs. It is a conveyor belt through which Russia turns Ukrainian children into Russian soldiers for a war against their own homeland. Britain has named those who run this conveyor belt from Crimea to Luhansk. We thank the United Kingdom: everyone who commits crimes against Ukrainian children must know that they will be held personally accountable," said Maksym Maksymov, head of Bring Kids Back UA.
The UK government said millions of Ukrainian children in the occupied territories are subjected to Kremlin propaganda programmes, including weapons training and drone operation. Their aim is to strip children of their Ukrainian identity and prepare them to serve the state attacking their homeland.
Those on the sanctions list have had their assets frozen, been banned from entering the UK, faced restrictions on trust services and been prohibited from serving as directors of companies.
Background:
- Defence Intelligence of Ukraine previously named 10 people involved in the militarisation of Ukrainian children in the occupied territories. They included Artur Orlov, Aleksei Lavrentyev, Riyal Aliyev, Yekaterina Kozyr and Viktoria Kostromina.
- The Russian curriculum is being imposed on almost 2,000 schools in Ukraine's temporarily occupied territories, shaping the education of over 582,000 children. Schools are introducing new subjects that emphasise "patriotic" indoctrination and cultivate loyalty to the Russian state ideology.
- Russian forces are actively militarising children in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, including through Yunarmiya and cadet classes. Another tool is the Movement of the First, which regularly holds military-style games and public ceremonies for handing out Russian IDs. More than 340,000 children and young people from the occupied territories are among its participants.

articles.title: Latvian PM faces bittersweet victory in election backdropped by Russia
articles.body:
RIGA — Latvia’s populist Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs will face his first electoral test Saturday — but his head start in the polls is unlikely to shield him from coalition headaches in a contest where Ukraine and Russia are looming large.
After a campaign partially fought in Brussels’ corridors, Kulbergs could see two of his allied parties fail to reach the 5% threshold to get seats. And if his centrist allies fail to make it into parliament, the pro-Ukraine prime minister might struggle to get enough backing.
In this worst-case scenario, he may even need to open talks with Ainārs Šlesers, a right-wing veteran of Latvian politics who opposed restrictive tariffs on Russia.
